News.title: Eclipse - live: How to make pinhole solar eclipse viewer as exact times revealed
News.content:
Brits are keeping their eyes peeled for the first near-total solar eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999 - with millions set to gather to view the astronomical phenomenon

Brits are counting down to a spectacular celestial show today as the Moon slides in front of the Sun in the UK's first near-total solar eclipse in over half a century.

The rare event will see daylight dim as the Moon blocks out more than 90% of the Sun in Britain, creating a fascinating crescent-shape in the evening sky.

Exact timings will depend on where you're located and can be seen in full here, but the event will begin shortly after 6pm, with the maximum eclipse occurring at shortly after 7pm before the Sun gradually re-emerges. In London, the eclipse will sweep in at 6.17pm, peak at 7.13pm and end at 8.06pm.

Experts have warned that looking directly at the Sun without proper protection can cause permanent eye damage and ordinary sunglasses are not enough. Only special solar eclipse glasses that are ISO 12312-2 certified should be used - eclipse glasses that do not carry the safety standards, or ordinary sunglasses, should never be used as they reduce glare, making it feel more comfortable to look at the Sun for longer, but still allow harmful solar radiation to reach the retina.

A pinhole viewer can be put together at home with just a cardboard box, kitchen foil and scissors as quick an easy alternative for viewing this evening's spectacle.

News.title: Boots issues important 'couldn’t be confident' update for customers using weight loss injections
News.content:
Boots issues important 'couldn’t be confident' update for customers using weight loss injections

'Patient safety has to come first', the high street pharmacy said

View Image Boots is pausing its delivery of weight loss jabs

Boots is temporarily pausing home delivery of weight loss injections during the heatwave due to safety concerns, it has said. The pharmacy chain said it had made the decision in order to keep the medication safe in transit amid temperatures set to exceed 30C across the country.

‌



It followed new testing by the Boots Online Doctor service that found cold chain packaging could not reliably keep weight loss injections within their required temperature range once outdoor temperatures exceeded 30C. It is advising patients to collect their medication from a local Boots store instead.

‌



Weight loss injections such as Wegovy and Mounjaro must be kept below 8C to maintain their quality and effectiveness, but Boots said the gel-pack cold chain packaging used across the industry to transport medications that require refrigeration had never been tested above 30C – despite the increasing frequency of UK heatwaves.

‌



Eight tests sent out by Boots on June 25, coinciding with outdoor temperatures exceeding 30C the next day, found each one recorded temperatures above 8C on arrival, indicating that standard packaging could not consistently keep the medication within its required temperature range throughout transit.

The chain said it had already temporarily paused its home deliveries of the jabs on several occasions this summer as successive heatwaves hit the UK. It said new packaging was expected to be introduced in the coming weeks, enabling the medication to be sent out at temperatures of up to 35C.

‌



Mandeep Kaur, pharmacist lead for the weight loss service at Boots Online Doctor, said: “Weight loss injections are sensitive to temperature. It’s important to store them as recommended, since exposure to temperatures outside the recommended range may affect the medicine’s quality and effectiveness.

“We’d always encourage patients to check their medication when it arrives and before administering them: look out for the solution appearing cloudy, discoloured or containing visible particles, or the packaging feeling warm to the touch on arrival. If in doubt, don’t use it and contact your provider.

“This is exactly why we’ve made the decision to temporarily pause deliveries during this summer’s heatwaves rather than risk sending out medication we couldn’t be confident had stayed within the recommended temperature range, which may impact its effectiveness and quality.

Article continues below

“Patient safety has to come first, even if that means a short-term inconvenience. It’s also worth knowing that not all weight loss injections have identical storage requirements – some brands allow a little more flexibility once they’re out of the fridge than some other brands.

“But the margin isn’t unlimited, and once the medication has been exposed to temperatures above 30C, it needs to be checked and replaced if it is not suitable for use, rather than relying on that flexibility to cover for a hot delivery.”

News.title: NHS must plan for heatwaves like winter crises to protect frail and vulnerable, Yvette Cooper says
News.content:
NHS must plan for heatwaves like winter crises to protect frail and vulnerable, Yvette Cooper says

EXCLUSIVE: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper admitted the sweltering conditions make things 'much more difficult' for those in care, as well as for staff looking after them

View 3 Images Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the hot weather puts at risk the same people - the elderly, those with existing conditions - who are affected by the cold in winter (Image: Getty Images)

Yvette Cooper has vowed to address challenges facing the “frail and vulnerable” in hospitals and care homes as staff battle yet another heatwave.

‌



The Health Secretary admitted the sweltering conditions make things "much more difficult" for those in care, as well as for staff looking after them.

‌



The Cabinet minister has ordered the NHS to start drawing up summer plans to deal with heatwaves as they traditionally do for winter crises. She said the hot weather puts at risk the same people - the elderly, young children and those with existing conditions - who are affected by the cold in winter.

‌



Writing for The Mirror, Ms Cooper said: "The extreme heat makes things much more difficult for all those who need care, and all those looking after them. And it is another reason why Andy Burnham is right to say we need major reform in social care, giving the care workforce the tools and support they need for every challenge they face, and lifting up the importance of care work in our national life."

UK heatwave to remain until September with fears of more drought and death toll set to be highest on record READ MORE :

View 3 Images Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the NHS is going to need 'the same level of preparation in future summers' as in the winters (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Wire)

Ms Cooper continued: “Our NHS is used to gearing up for these kinds of pressures in winter. But we are going to need the same level of preparation in future summers. I have told the NHS to start drawing up summer plans now in the way they have traditionally done for winter.

‌



“Especially as all the same people who are most at risk when it is very cold are at risk in the extreme heat: older people, the youngest children, and people with existing conditions. That means effective planning in emergency care, hospitals and care homes – especially supporting those who are frail and vulnerable.”

Ms Cooper added that £6.75billion was already being invested to improve NHS buildings, including better cooling.

Latest data shows around 2,800 lives were lost because of the extreme heat during the May and June heatwaves, with 2026 on track to see the highest ever number of heat-related deaths. Around 60% of the excess deaths were of people aged 85 and over, analysis by Imperial University found.

‌



View 3 Images Latest data shows around 2,800 lives were lost because of the extreme heat during the May and June heatwaves (Image: NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Dennis Reed, director of Silver Voices, which represents senior UK citizens, called for heatwaves to receive the same response as winter.

He told The Mirror: "Extreme heat should be treated with the same vigour as extreme cold, unfortunately it is not.

‌



“Older bodies cannot regulate heat as well as the young; and many are dying of heat-induced complications from chronic heart, respiratory and cardio-vascular conditions, or dehydration. This should be treated as a national emergency.”

He continued: “I have had complaints from members that they cannot afford to run fans because of the exorbitant energy prices, and there should be a cold homes allowance for pensioners to match the warm homes payment system.

“Most care homes do not have air conditioning and, with closed windows for security, act like furnaces. The Care Quality Commission should pick up preparations for heatwaves when it inspects care homes."

‌



Nadra Ahmed, co-chair of the National Care Association, which represents care providers, said it has not been the “norm” for care homes to have air conditioning unless they have a newer purpose-built service.

She said, over the course of this year’s heatwaves, care homes have been looking to purchase air conditioning units to at least keep some rooms cool but availability has been an issue.

“I think it is on the radar but of course the units are not available anymore,” she said.

‌



“I've had a lot of providers saying to me it's been really difficult to go and get the kind of units and then the fitting, because we're not the only sector, everybody’s affected. You know, offices are doing it. There's a huge amount of interest in getting these units in.”

She said care homes have also been investing in cooling packs to put in freezers or putting cold wet flannels around people’s necks to “try to make life as comfortable as we possibly can”.

Ms Ahmed said she was more concerned about those who have in-home carers visit them.

‌



She continued: “I think the bigger worry I have is people who are living alone, and the home care market, because of course people are only going in there for 15/20 minutes.

“You can't have all the windows open in the evening to try and get some cool air in because of the risks attached to that.”

Dr Deb Gompertz, the British Geriatrics Society’s honorary secretary and vice president for policy, said: “Heat is the most dangerous climate-related threat to life in the UK, and older people are the most likely to die because of extreme heat. The vast majority of hospitals in England are vulnerable to overheating.

‌



Steps need to be taken at a system level to adapt NHS and social care facilities to the effects of climate change. These measures are long-term, and so they must be started as soon as possible. The Government, local authorities and NHS Trusts must equip their estates and workforce to provide safe care during extreme heat.

Age UK urges people to visit or check by phone on neighbours or relatives who live alone and who are living with frailty or with health issues.

It also recommends older people stay inside during the hottest time of the day and when inside, trying to keep your house cool by keeping curtains and blinds closed in rooms that catch the sun and shut windows during the day to keep hot air out and cool air in.

‌



Chris Badger, Chief Inspector of Adult Social Care and Integrated Care at the Care Quality Commission, said: “Providers are required to ensure that premises, equipment and environmental conditions support the delivery of safe care, with effective arrangements in place to monitor and respond to risks such as high temperatures.

“When we assess services, we look at how they protect people from environmental risks and ensure their individual needs are met during periods of extreme heat. If we find providers are not meeting this requirement we can take regulatory action.”

'NHS must prepare for heatwaves as they do with winter planning'

By Health Secretary Yvette Cooper

‌



I can still remember, as a seven-year-old girl, the scorching summer of 1976.

Elton John and Kiki Dee were at Number 1. Princess Anne was competing for Britain at the Olympics. And for fifteen consecutive days, temperatures rose above 32°C – making it the hottest summer on record.

Until now. We have already had 34 days this year with temperatures 30°C or above, and this week has seen yet another official heatwave.

‌



Fifty years ago, we knew we were facing something exceptional. But now, with climate change affecting the entire planet, we are having to face the idea that these kinds of temperatures will become the norm. And that has major implications for our nation’s health.

During the heatwaves in May and June, we saw more than 2,800 lives lost because of the extreme heat, and this year is on track to see the highest ever number of heat-related deaths. My thoughts go out to every family who has lost loved ones.

I have seen for myself the impact that the extreme heat is having on our NHS, with A&E units under increased pressure across the whole country.

‌



I am incredibly grateful to the hospital staff and emergency responders who have worked tirelessly to protect people through these challenging months.

Our NHS is used to gearing up for these kinds of pressures in winter. But we are going to need the same level of preparation in future summers. I have told the NHS to start drawing up summer plans now in the way they have traditionally done for winter.

Especially as all the same people who are most at risk when it is very cold are at risk in the extreme heat: older people, the youngest children, and people with existing conditions.

‌



That means effective planning in emergency care, hospitals and care homes – especially supporting those who are frail and vulnerable.

The extreme heat makes things much more difficult for all those who need care, and all those looking after them. And it is another reason why Andy Burnham is right to say we need major reform in social care, giving the care workforce the tools and support they need for every challenge they face, and lifting up the importance of care work in our national life.

We will also need to make sure buildings can adapt to heat as well as cold – already we are investing £6.75 billion to tackle the most serious problems across the NHS estate, including better cooling.

Article continues below

As this hot summer continues, better prevention will be crucial too. There is good advice on the NHS website especially during heat alerts. But this is also a good time for all of us to do our bit by checking in on elderly neighbours, families with young children, or those who need a little extra help.

Just like we would if the temperatures were freezing instead.

In 1976, a summer like this felt extraordinary. Half a century later, it doesn’t. We know Britain will face heatwaves like this with increasing frequency and increasing intensity. So we have to take the health consequences much more seriously, so that everyone is ready when they come.

News.title: Dr Amir Khan shares 'brilliant' way to watch eclipse as normal sunglasses 'not enough'
News.content:
Dr Amir Khan shares 'brilliant' way to watch eclipse as normal sunglasses 'not enough'

The UK is set to experience its biggest eclipse since 1999 within hours

View 3 Images Dr Amir Khan (Image: Getty)

TV doctor Amir Khan has shared his "brilliant" way of viewing the eclipse which is due to happen in the UK in hours. Starting at about 6pm tonight the Moon will begin moving across the face of the Sun, which will mean a partial solar eclipse across the UK.

‌



According to Royal Museums Greenwich (RMG), at its peak, up to 95% of the Sun will be hidden in Cornwall while viewers in Pembrokeshire will see 94%. For those in the south-western tip of Ireland, it might even be as much as almost 97.5% coverage.

‌



It added when the eclipse will be visible will depend on your location, travelling from the north to the south. It will begin between 6.08pm and 6.18pm and end between 8pm and 8.10pm however the maximum eclipse is expected between 7.05pm and 7.16pm.

‌



View 3 Images Stargazers are counting down the hours until the eclipse (stock photo) (Image: Getty)

On August 11, 1999 the UK experienced its last total solar eclipse which was was viewed by millions of people. While today's will not be a total eclipse it is still expected to see crowds enjoying the experience.

Now GMB and Lorraine doctor Amir Khan has warned people not to rely on one item to watch the phenomenon. He said: "Normal sunglasses are NOT enough. Use genuine eclipse glasses meeting ISO 12312-2.

‌



"Never look through binoculars/telescopes without a proper solar filter fitted to the front Be careful trying to photograph it. A pinhole projector is a brilliant, safe way to watch indirectly. Even a colander can project lots of tiny eclipses!

"Enjoy it. Marvel at it. Bore everyone with your eclipse photos afterwards. Just please protect those retinas while you’re doing it."

In a video he expanded his advice saying: "Please don't just go out and look at the sun because it can permanently damage your eyesight, and you may not even feel it happening until it's too late." He went on to share "five things you need to know" before looking at the eclipse.

‌



Normal sunglasses are not enough.

He said: "Doesn't matter how dark they are, no matter about their UV protection. It doesn't matter whether you look like a Gucci model whilst you're wearing them. If you want to look directly at the Eclipse, you need proper Eclipse glasses that meet the international safety standard.

View 3 Images Sunglasses are not enough says Dr Amir (Image: Getty Images)

"And if you've had your Eclipse glasses since 1999, then you need to check them first, make sure they're not scratched, torn, punctured, or damaged. If they are, don't use them."

‌



Do not improvise

He says makeshift ideas are not the right way forward. He explains: "Don't put on three pairs of sunglasses and think, ah, this is enough.

"Don't look through a CD or a DVD or smoke glass or a photographic film or crisp packets. I've heard everything. They're not designed to protect your retina from looking directly at the sun."

Your phone isn't automatically a safe workaround

The expert said: "Don't stare at the sun while you're trying to line up that perfect photograph. It's just not worth it. And don't look through a camera, binoculars, or telescope unless that equipment has a proper solar filter fitted to the front of it.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

"In fact, never put eclipse glasses on and then look through binoculars or a tele, even because that will concentrate the sunlight, and that can damage and the filter and your eyes."

The safest way to watch without looking at the sun

Dr Amir advises one thing is "really great" to do with kids. He says: "I know you sounds a bit Blue Petery. Make a pinhole projector. You can literally use two pieces of card make a tiny hole in one. Stand with your back to the sun and project the image onto the other.

‌



"Or here's a really good one I like to do with children. Hold up a kitchen colander and watch all those little pleasant suns appear in each shadow. Remember, you're watching a projection. You're not looking directly at the sun through that tiny pinhole."

What happens if you do actually stare at the sun?

Dr Amir also explains what happens if you do look into the sun. He says: "Well, you can develop something called solar retinopathy. The intense light damages the light-sensitive cells of the retina at the back of the eye.

"And the scary thing is, you might not even feel it while it's happening. You might just notice it later as a blurred spot in the middle of your vision, or just abnormal vision.

Article continues below

"And in some cases that is permanent. So we don't want that evil. So remember, go out, enjoy the eclipse. I'll be there watching it, but safely. Make sure you do it safely."

News.title: Genealogist who's seen 1,000s of baby names reveals bizarre one that 'takes some beating'
News.content:
Genealogist who's seen 1,000s of baby names reveals bizarre one that 'takes some beating'

A genealogist at the UK's leading probate firm has spent years poring over historical birth records and encountered countless strange baby names – but one extraordinary combination from the 1980s still takes some beating.

View 4 Images The record dates from the 1980s (Image: Rawlstock via Getty Images)

Unusual baby names are often dismissed as a modern phenomenon, but one genealogist has revealed that some truly extraordinary choices can be found in records stretching back generations.

‌



Neil Fraser, who runs Fraser and Fraser, the UK's leading probate genealogy firm, has spent years working with the documents that connect families across generations.

‌



The firm's work involves tracing relatives through records such as wills, birth certificates and marriage certificates, giving its experts an unusually detailed insight into the names people have been given over the years.

‌



And while some of the strangest examples might seem as though they belong firmly in the Victorian era, Neil said one of the most memorable records he has encountered came from much more recently.

He said: "When you spend as much time looking through historical records as we do, you quickly learn that unusual names are certainly not a modern invention."

Among the older records examined by Neil and his colleagues was one involving a girl born in 1875 who had been given the name Zebra.

‌



Another record, dating back to 1842, listed a child as Mineral Girl, while a child born in 1907 was given the first name Enough.

Elsewhere, the team found a birth record where the child's name was simply recorded as Baby Girl.

The unusual discoveries became even more remarkable in other cases.

‌



View 4 Images Neil said the sheer combination of names was difficult to forget (Image: Catherine Delahaye via Getty Images)

Neil said the genealogists had encountered a girl who appeared to have been given 26 names, following the alphabet from one name to the next.

They also came across an 1885 marriage involving Frankenstein Pitt and a woman who was already a Frankenstein herself.

‌



But despite the bizarre examples found in historic records, one of Neil's favourites came from the 1980s.

He said: "One of our favourites is much more recent, where we came across a birth record containing the forenames Buzz, Fly, Pineapple, Pedigree, Abbot, Whoopsie and Bun. Even after seeing thousands of records, that one takes some beating."

The combination was so unusual that it immediately stuck in his mind.

‌



"It's very difficult to beat a name like Buzz Fly Pineapple," he said.

What makes the record particularly striking is its age.

Rather than belonging to a Victorian child whose unusual name has survived only through an old document, the record dates from the 1980s.

‌



Neil said: "What makes it particularly memorable is that it isn't some eccentric Victorian curiosity. The record is from the 1980s. This person is likely still alive."

View 4 Images Neil Fraser

He added: "You expect the nineteenth century to occasionally throw something unusual at you, but seeing that combination on a comparatively modern birth record certainly makes you stop and read it twice."

‌



The discovery has even had an impact inside Fraser and Fraser, with two of the names becoming particular favourites among staff.

"We've seen thousands of names over the years, but Whoopsie and Pineapple have definitely become office favourites," Neil said.

The firm's experiences also show that unusual names aren't necessarily something people leave behind once they reach adulthood.

‌



Neil said the genealogists had encountered a number of people who had changed their names by Deed Poll.

The most memorable example, he said, was someone who had changed their given name to Sausage.

While Britain has its own rules around names and official records, some countries take a much stricter approach to what parents can call their children.

‌



One particularly unusual case occurred in Norway after a mother attempted to register her son under the name Gesher, which means bridge in Hebrew.

View 4 Images In another case, a child was recorded simply as Baby Girl.

According to Erin McCarthy, speaking on the YouTube channel Mental Floss: "Norway is yet another country that regulates what parents can name their child. One Norwegian mother was fined about $210 for using the unapproved name 'Gesher,' and sent to jail when she didn't pay. She protested, saying that she had been instructed to name her son Gesher, the Hebrew word for bridge, in a dream she had."

‌



The woman, Kirsti Larsen, had 14 children and said the dream came shortly before the birth of her 13th child in April 1995.

She claimed a voice had instructed her in English to call the baby "Bridge", leading her to choose the Hebrew translation, Gesher.

But Norwegian officials rejected the name.

Article continues below

Authorities argued that it was too foreign, was not sufficiently recognisable as a boy's name and was too close to the surname Geser.

Norway's naming laws date back to the 19th century and give authorities the power to reject names considered inappropriate or likely to cause difficulties for a child.

For genealogists, cases like these provide an unusual insight into the way parents have made naming decisions across different periods – and show that unusual baby names are certainly not a purely modern trend.

News.title: Solar eclipse to spark power shortage for three hours tonight
News.content:
Solar eclipse to spark power shortage for three hours tonight

The UK's growing reliance on solar farms to generate electricity has prompted the UK's system operator to take action to avoid any risk of blackouts

View 3 Images The solar eclipse is eagerly anticipated - but has caused a headache for power bosses (Image: ©2025 George Pachantouris)

Britain’s electricity system operator has issued a plea for more power during this evening’s solar eclipse. The National Energy System Operator (Neso) said there would be a shortage of spare capacity between 6pm and 10pm.

‌



It comes as the UK experiences its fullest solar eclipse for the next 54 years, as millions of people across Europe are expected to gather to watch the Sun, the Moon and the Earth line up.

‌



More than 90% of the Sun will be obscured by the Moon between 6.17pm and 8.06pm, the most it has been blocked above UK skies since the total eclipse in 1999.

‌



View 3 Images Solar farms are part of the UK's growing use of renewable power (Image: PA Archive/PA Images)

Avoid using washing machines and dishwashers during solar eclipse, Octopus urges READ MORE :

What time is solar eclipse today in UK and best places to watch – complete guide READ MORE :

However, since then, the UK - and the rest of Europe - has become ever more reliant on solar power to produce electricity.

NESO issued an “electricity margin notice” for between 6pm and 8pm on Wednesday, when there is an expected shortfall of 1,200 megawatts compared with the amount it would like to be available.

‌



The move is an alert to other energy generators to activate any additional capacity they have.

On Tuesday evening, NESO had warned the shortfall could last from 5pm to 8pm, saying the buffer against an electricity shortage could end 1,760 megawatts below the desired amount.

View 3 Images Millions are awaiting the rare sight of a solar eclipse (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



A NESO spokesperson said: “We have used our routine tool of issuing an Electricity Margin Notice (EMN) for tomorrow evening’s peak, which simply means we are asking market participants to make any additional generation capacity they may have available.

“The notice has been issued as a precautionary measure to the market due to the solar eclipse and there is no risk to customer electricity supplies.”

Octopus Energy, Britain’s biggest electricity provider, is urging its customer to use less power during the solar eclipse.

‌



As a reward for doing this, the supplier said it will give customers who are signed up to its “savings sessions” scheme a free hour of electricity to use next weekend.

During the celestial event, the amount of solar power generation will temporarily drop - and this will happen at the peak time in the evening when households are home and using energy-heavy appliances.

The notice issued on Tuesday night is the fourth EMN the grid operator has put out this year.

Article continues below

Jess Ralston, head of energy at think tank the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, said: “The National Energy System Operator’s electricity margin notice is a standard tool it frequently uses to ask for more power to be available because of tighter margins – it’s a precaution that gives them some extra buffer.

“Today’s eclipse will mean solar power goes offline earlier than usual and coincides with peak electricity demand so having more power sources available on standby is part of running a robust grid, with the UK’s being one of the most reliable in the world while increasingly going green.

“This year has seen more margin notices issued in the summer because of the frequent heatwaves, which are being made worse and more common by climate change, as extreme heat drives up demand from air con and fans while reducing efficiency of many power sources including gas and nuclear. The only way to bring our climate back into balance is to reach net zero emissions, including rolling out more renewables and upgrading the grid after decades of under investment.”

News.title: Julie Andrews' announces retirement from acting: 'It's been a wonderful ride'
News.content:
Julie Andrews' announces retirement from acting: 'It's been a wonderful ride'

Iconic actress Julie Andrews, 90, has shared that she has retired from onscreen acting appearances and will not appear in The Princess Diaries 3, as she rejected returning as Queen Clarisse

View 4 Images Julie Andrews on The Graham Norton Show (Image: PA)

Julie Andrews has announced her retirement from acting onscreen after rejecting a return to The Princess Diaries. The 90-year-old has enoyed a near 80-year career, and starred in hit movies from Mary Poppins to The Sound of Music and amassed multiple awards, including three Emmys, two Grammys, and an Oscar.

‌



However, now Julie has revealed she is taking a huge step back, confirming her on-screen days are over

‌



Julie said retirement was the "best description" for how she was approaching her career. She made the statement after being asked if she would return with the rest of the cast for the third Princess Diaries' film.

‌



Movie fans poke fun at Anne Hathaway after 'horrifying' Verity trailer released READ MORE :

The Odyssey star Samantha Morton still 'hurt' after being replaced by Scarlett Johansson in huge film READ MORE :

4 View 4 Images Julie Andrews in the Sound of Music (Image: Getty Images) 4 View 4 Images Julie with Anne Hathaway at the Princess Diaries 2 premiere (Image: Getty Images)

Julie said film bosses had asked her "all last year if I would be keen" and that she found it difficult to refuse.

The star told InStyle Magazine acting had been a "wonderful ride" but felt she was too old now to appear on camera.

‌



The last time Julie acted on-screen was 2010, when she appeared as Lily, the head fairy in Dwayne Johnson's Tooth Fairy. She has made appearances as herself in various TV shows, but the majority of her work in the past 16 years has been voice acting. She has voiced Lady Whistledown on Bridgerton since 2020 and most recently voiced Marlena in Minions: The Rise of Gru in 2022.

Julie said she is more happy to keep doing voice acting, as she can record her lines from the comfort of her own home. "I do it mostly to keep my brain alive," she admitted.

View 4 Images Julie Andrews in 2019 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



In The Princess Diaries, Julie played Queen Clarisse, the grandmother of Anne Hathaway's Mia, a San Franciscan student who finds out that she is actually the heir to the throne of a small European nation. The news that Julie won't do another Princess Diaries film will surely be sad to Anne, who previously told Entertainment Tonight that she wanted Julie to come back for a third film.

"We would go to where she was and put a green screen behind her and just make it happen," Anne said. Anne is set to reprise her role as Queen Mia Thermopolis in the film.

Though she kept the details under wraps, she told SiriusXM that the filmmakers had to "start over" with their script and go in a "new direction". She continued: "But we all feel really good that this is gonna be the one."

‌



Julie's recent words comes just a few months after she made a rare public appearance to raise awareness for Parkinson's. She appeared in a video to launch the World Parkinson's Congress conference. In the video, the British star explained that she knows first-hand just how "devastating" the condition can be for people.

Speaking in the video, shared on YouTube by the World Parkinson Coalition, she said: "Good evening, everyone, I'm Julie Andrews, and I'm pleased to welcome you to the seventh World Parkinson's Congress. Your participation is invaluable as we seek to find a cure to this terrible disease. I know well how devastating it can be."

Julie has battled her own health issues over the years. She was forced to quit a stage production of Victor/Victoria back in 1997 when she developed a hoarseness in her throat and underwent surgery to remove "a cyst" from her vocal cord. She told AARP The Magazine in 2019 that, when she woke up, her singing voice was gone.

Article continues below

"I went into a depression," she said. "It felt like I'd lost my identity." In 1999, Julie filed a malpractice lawsuit against the doctors who performed the surgery. Ten years later, she revealed that the non-cancerous nodules she thought were being removed from her throat at the time didn't actually exist and that she had instead been suffering from "a certain kind of muscular striation".

The actress has since had several operations to repair her voice. "Do I miss singing?" she asked herself. "Yes I really do. I would have been quite a sad lady if I hadn't had the voice to hold on to."

News.title: Four men killed in Huyton crash 'identified by dental records' after car hit lamppost
News.content:
Four men killed in Huyton crash 'identified by dental records' after car hit lamppost

Jack Diggle, 23, Ben Dooley, 23, Andrew Roberts, 24, and Craig Shackleton-Brady, 26, died from 'multiple injuries' in the crash and were identified by dental records

Huyton: Police at scene of serious crash in July

Four men who were killed after their car slammed into a lamppost in Huyton were identified by dental records after dying from "multiple injuries", a coroner's court has heard.

Jack Diggle, 23, Benjamin Dooley, 23, Andrew Roberts, 24, and Craig Shackleton-Brady, 26, were all pronounced dead at the scene when police were called to reports that a Seat Cupra Formentor had come off the road on East Prescot Road in the early hours of July 24.

Opening their inquests at Bootle Town Hall today, senior coroner for Sefton Anita Bhardwaj heard the four men were identified by their dental records, as well as by clothing which they were seen to be wearing on CCTV footage earlier in the evening.

View 6 Images All four men were pronounced dead at the scene (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Coroner's officer Liam Moss told the court the single-vehicle collision happened at 1.54am on the eastbound carriageway of the road.

He said: "The collision resulted in the deaths of four of the five occupants of the vehicle."

View 6 Images Jack Diggle (Image: Merseyside Police/PA Wire)

The cause of death for the four men was given as multiple injuries.

The brief hearing was told Mr Dooley, of Stockbridge Village, was a student and Mr Shackleton-Brady, from Dovecot, was a warehouse operative.

View 6 Images Craig Shackleton-Brady (Image: Merseyside Police/PA Wire)

Mr Diggle, of West Derby, and Mr Roberts, of Dovecot, were both unemployed, the court heard.

James Diggle, 27, of West Derby, has been charged with four counts of aiding and abetting causing death by dangerous driving and is due to appear at Liverpool Crown Court next month.

Ms Bhardwaj formally opened the inquests and suspended them to await the outcome of criminal proceedings.

View 6 Images Andrew Roberts (Image: Merseyside Police/PA Wire)

Jack Diggle's mum said the 23-year-old's death had "left a hole" in the lives and hearts of those around him that can "never be filled".

The family said Jack was a proud Everton FC supporter who had a passion for watching and playing darts and was blessed with a "wonderful" group of friends, reports the Liverpool Echo.

"We will carry him with us every day and miss him for the rest of our lives," they said.

Benjamin Dooley's mum said her son was the "kindest person I knew with a heart of gold," while his sister Demi remembered him as "the one who always gave me advice and looked out for me, the most caring, kindest person in the world".

View 6 Images Benjamin Dooley (Image: Merseyside Police/PA Wire)

She added: "My heart is broken."

Andrew Roberts' mum said her life will "will never be the same" after losing her "beautiful blue-eyed boy".

‌



Andrew's dad said: "You were the world to me...and the best son anyone could ask for. I can't imagine life without you."

His brothers, Carl and Thomas, remembered "Pip" as the "glue to our crazy family".

Craig Shackleton-Brady's sister, Kelsey, said her younger brother, who worked as a warehouse operator, was "one of the kindest and gentlest people you could ever meet."

‌



His long-term partner, Ellie Jones, who was also the mum of their young children, Phoebe and Archie, said: "He was my life, my rock. I don't know life without him."

View 6 Images Police at the cordoned off scene on Liverpool Road (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Following the confirmation of James Diggle's charge, a Merseyside Police spokesperson said: "As criminal proceedings are now active, we would ask that the public refrain from commenting on, or speculating about, the circumstances of this case online, as this could unintentionally prejudice the judicial process.

Article continues below

"Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the four men who tragically lost their lives and we ask that their privacy is respected at this extremely difficult time."

News.title: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses
News.content:
With most online orders not able to arrive in time and shops running out of stock, it may be too late to buy eclipse glasses for Wednesday evening.

But you can still safely watch the spectacle using some household items.

People in the UK will see a partial eclipse - rather than the total eclipse that will be seen in parts of Spain, Greenland and Iceland - but it is the country's most significant eclipse since 1999.

Experts say enthusiasts should not look directly at the Sun without specialist glasses.

And you shouldn't be tempted to try using sunglasses or dark goggles instead.

They often don't give enough UV protection when looking directly at the Sun and you could end up seriously damaging your eyesight, according to The Royal Astronomical Society.

Here are some viewing methods to try instead.

News.title: Burnham says disposable BBQ ban under consideration
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the government is considering a ban on disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

Some retailers have already decided to voluntarily stop selling the devices, which have previously attracted warnings from fire chiefs.

It comes as Burnham chairs an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures in recent months.

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

Speaking during a visit to Stevenage, Burnham said a disposable barbecue ban was something the government was "certainly going to consider".

"I do want to leave the meeting today with a loud and clear message that we do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires," he added.

News.title: Early release scheme risks more serious crimes, probation chief warns
News.content:
The chief inspector of probation for England and Wales has told the BBC the early release of thousands of prisoners could lead to "a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder" because of the demands on probation staff to monitor offenders.

The government is set to release 5,000 offenders from October as part of new laws to create more space in overcrowded prisons.

Probation officers supervise offenders after prison sentences and check they follow the terms of their release, such as sticking to curfews and not taking drugs.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "protecting the public is our top priority", adding it had invested in probation and hiring trainee officers.

But Martin Jones, His Majesty's Chief Inspector of probation for England and Wales, told the BBC that "ultimately I'm not fully confident that the probation system will be able to cope with this massive work and there's a risk that things will go wrong".

"Probation services are already under unprecedented pressure.

"I mean, they're managing a caseload of 258,000 cases, that's nearly three times the number that are in our prisons, and obviously the early release scheme will be increasing that pressure considerably."

On Tuesday, 50 police chiefs across the UK signed a letter to the prime minister urging him to pursue "every legal option" to prevent the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers under the scheme.

They called for called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered, adding: "Families across the country are now facing the distress of learning that offenders may be released earlier than they understood when sentence was passed."

They also welcomed Burnham's intervention on Tuesday, when he said he was "confident" the early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were jailed for 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, in January could be stopped.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp told BBC Breakfast the early release plans had "put public safety at risk as well as disrespecting victims and undermining confidence in the criminal justice system".

He urged Burnham to "pay attention and listen" to the senior police officers, adding he had "never seen every chief constable in the country write to the prime minister directly in this way".

Philip and Nick Timothy, the Conservative shadow justice secretary, wrote to Burnham on Tuesday urging him to introduce emergency primary legislation in September to amend the Sentencing Act 2026.

The letter said grooming gang perpetrators, including those convicted of indecent assault, and those convicted of the manslaughter of an emergency worker should be exempt from the early release scheme.

News.title: Serious failings found in new military crimes unit, leaked report finds
News.content:
A leaked Ministry of Defence (MoD) report, obtained by the BBC, has highlighted serious failings in a new military command set up to investigate the most severe crimes, including rape and sexual assault.

The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) was launched after the death of 19-year-old Gunner Jaysley Beck. An inquest found the Army's mishandling of sexual assault and harassment complaints made by Beck contributed to her taking her own life, and exposed "systemic failings".

However, an internal review highlighted ongoing concerns with the unit and warned the military still risks failing victims.

The MoD said the findings had been accepted and significant work has been undertaken since.

The DSCC was created in 2022 to investigate serious crimes independently, outside the military's chain of command.

However, the BBC can reveal that an internal review, which was carried out between 21 August 2025 and 12 November 2025 and overseen by a former senior civilian police officer, concluded that if the DSCC was subjected to scrutiny similar to civilian police forces there would be "a significant risk of (it) being graded as inadequate".

In a statement, the MoD said the review was commissioned "to provide honest challenge, identify areas of improvement and to help ensure the highest standards for victims and witnesses".

It added that following the findings, the DSCC had carried out significant work "including further investment in victim and witness support, strengthening governance and safeguarding arrangements and accrediting investigators to nationally recognised policing standards".

The DSCC was committed to transparency, continuous improvement and ensuring victims receive the support and service they deserve, the statement continued.

News.title: Homes near pylons to get £250 a year off energy bills – first sites revealed
News.content:
UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast the UK's power infrastructure had undergone decades of "woeful underinvestment".

He said he understood the objections of those living nearby, but added the pylons were "crucial" to ensure the National Grid maintained future resilience.

"I totally accept that people might not like that, but it is critical national infrastructure and it has to be built somewhere," he said.

"Building any kind of infrastructure in these communities does cause disruption. But that doesn't mean we shouldn't build any kind of infrastructure and I'm afraid in this country, for too long, we have taken that view, and the result is that we have been held back by not having the infrastructure the country needs."

Shanks added: "Either we go through decades of not upgrading the grid and take the risk that the grid will actually fail, but we also lose the opportunity of cheaper bills, homegrown power connecting.

"We're not prepared to take that risk."

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero says Britain's electricity grid was largely designed for an era when power came from coal and gas-fired power stations, and now needs major upgrades to cope with growing amounts of renewable energy.

Ministers say the lack of capacity means some wind farms are sometimes paid to switch off because there is not enough network infrastructure available to carry the electricity to homes and businesses that need it.

Greg Jackson, chief executive of the UK's biggest domestic energy supplier, Octopus Energy, said the electricity system is inefficient, brittle and expensive.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the discount scheme was a "positive first step", adding that last year the UK spent more than Â£1bn paying wind farms to turn off on windy days.

"We should just be giving that electricity more cheaply to the people and businesses who live in the areas where we're generating it," he said.

"By doing that, you'd be able to stop wasting that money and instead put the electricity to use cutting bills for those people. But crucially cutting bills for everybody else as well because it's less wasteful."

News.title: X-Men star Nicholas Hoult joins cast of Harry Potter TV show
News.content:
Nicholas Hoult, known for his roles in X-Men, Superman and Mad Max: Fury Road, has been cast in the hotly anticipated Harry Potter TV series.

The English actor, 36, will play Hogwarts professor Gilderoy Lockhart - who was portrayed by Sir Kenneth Branagh in the films.

The TV adaptation of JK Rowling's best-selling books will reach screens this Christmas, although Hoult will not be seen until season two.

In the stories, Lockhart was a celebrity author of books such as Magical Me before joining Hogwarts as a Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher in Harry's second year.

HBO announced the casting, external by quoting the title of Lockhart's autobiography and one of his famous lines: "Magical me indeed. Now, how many autographs would you like? Nicholas Hoult has been cast as Gilderoy Lockhart in season two of the new HBO original Harry Potter series."

News.title: Spotify to add label for AI-generated artists and remove them from recommendations
News.content:
Spotify is introducing a new feature that will highlight if an artist has been generated by artificial intelligence (AI).

The streaming service says the AI Persona badge, that will start appearing on some profiles from mid-September, will flag to listeners if an "artist's identity may be AI-generated and does not represent a real person".

The changes are being introduced to give listeners "more transparency" about what they're hearing, Spotify says.

It comes after some music fans made it "clear" to the streamer they don't like seeing a profile that seems to be a human, to then realise it's AI-generated.

AI-generated music has long been a concern for users of the platform.

The BBC previously heard from one frustrated listener, who, after finding his playlists increasingly sprinkled with tracks he suspected were AI-generated, built a tool to automatically label and block them.

Announcing the change, external, Spotify says "true artist-fan connection can only be built on a foundation of trust and authenticity".

"In music, that means listeners need to be able to trust that the artist behind the music is who they say they are," it adds.

"That's more essential than ever in the age of generative AI."

News.title: How the weather will affect your viewing
News.content:
One of the most spectacular solar eclipses the UK has seen for decades is taking place on Wednesday 12 August.

From around 18:00 BST, the Moon will begin moving across the face of the Sun, creating a partial solar eclipse across the UK.

At its peak, around 90% of the Sun will be covered from London. In Cornwall, as much as 95% of the Sun could be obscured.

Depending on where you are in the UK, it will peak between 19:02 and 19:16 BST.

News.title: Burnham to chair Cobra meeting on extreme heat as temperatures surge again
News.content:
The Cobra meeting will be attended by ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Home Office, and Department for Health, as well as the Environment Agency.

It will be the second Cobra meeting this year on heatwaves, after one took place amid high temperatures in June.

A spokesperson for No 10 said this summer was proving "challenging" in the UK, particularly for "firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units".

"We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment," they said.

The hottest weather this week is expected on Thursday across the Midlands, Eastern England, London and south-east England, Yorkshire and Humber.

Temperatures could potentially reach 38C which would equal the highest temperature of the summer so far recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk on 26 June.

This would be the hottest August day since 2003, when 38.5C was recorded.

It is also likely to be the fourth calendar month this year to record 35C or more, which is unprecedented.

On Monday, drought officials declared 71.3% of England in drought, meaning there are a total of 45 million people now living in a drought area, with more than 27 million facing water use restrictions.

Firefighters have responded to 966 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August, and 458 in July, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council.

A fire in the New Forest has been burning since Sunday, which started after a van caught fire on the A31 near Ringwood.

Last week, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the NHS should be "preparing for summer pressures now in the same way we prepare for winter".

She told LBC Radio plans were in place to respond to higher numbers of people coming in to A&E.

On Tuesday, the Met Office said this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, with the mean temperature currently at 16.48C set to surpass the figure set just last year.

This is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the Cobra meeting was just a first step, and a "climate emergency" had led to hundreds of deaths and was "stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit".

He called for "concrete action" and said he looked forward to hearing how Burnham intended to "prepare for the threats to come".

News.title: Scotland's public spending deficit falls as tax take rises
News.content:
Scotland's public spending deficit fell by Â£600m last year to Â£25.3bn after an increase in the amount raised in taxes, figures show.

The annual Government Expenditure and Revenue Scotland (Gers) report compares the tax raised in Scotland with public spending for and on behalf of Scotland.

It said that revenue had grown by Â£6.3bn to Â£98.3bn, an increase of 6.9%, while there was a slower growth in expenditure, which rose by Â£5.7bn to Â£123.6bn - an increase of 4.8%.

The largest increases in revenue came from national insurance contributions, which were up by Â£2.4bn, and income tax receipts, up by Â£1.5bn.

The expenditure of Â£123.6bn is the amount spent by the Scottish, UK and local governments north of the border - as well as a share of spending on shared provision such as defence and debt.

News.title: 102-year-old man in critical condition after alleged pub assault
News.content:
A 102-year-old man is in a critical condition after allegedly being assaulted at a pub.

Emergency services were called to The Crow's Nest pub in Cwmbran, Torfaen, at about 22:25 BST on 1 August, and the man was taken to hospital.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm, and has since been released under investigation.

Gwent Police is appealing for witnesses and want to speak to anyone who was in the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 on the night of the incident.

News.title: Four guilty over torture death of man set alight
News.content:
Four people have been found guilty over charges relating to the death of a man doused in petrol and set on fire.

Tomasz Samel was kidnapped in 2019 from his home in Birmingham by an organised crime group who believed he was responsible for the loss of Â£1m worth of illicit cigarettes. He was driven to the Liverpool area and brutally attacked.

Tobiasz Kozlowski, of Kirby, Merseyside, and Neil Jones, 48, of no fixed address were found guilty of murder following the death of the 45-year-old who was kidnapped, falsely imprisoned, tortured and set on fire.

Two more men, Kevin Wooden, of Banbury, Oxfordshire, and Kye Arthur, from Bristol, were cleared of murder but found guilty of manslaughter.

Samel was kidnapped from his Handsworth home by Wooden and Arthur and a third male. They had posed as Interpol officers executing a European arrest warrant.

The father of two was subjected to violence before being set on fire and then later left by a roadside in Lancashire. He had been able to knock on the door of a nearby remote house and told the residents he had been driven from Birmingham and tortured.

He died from his injuries in hospital about three months later.

Kozlowski's wife, Sandra Kozlowska, 38, also from Kirkby, was convicted of assisting an offender after she helped her husband to avoid suspicion by depositing money in bank accounts for him and lying to the police.

Kozlowski and Jones recruited others to help kidnap, imprison and inflict serious violence on him as punishment.

Kate Seal, from the Crown Prosecution Service said Samel was subjected to "horrendous violence" and what happened to him was a "brutal attack".

"Our thoughts remain with Mr Samel's family, who have endured unimaginable suffering, including witnessing his abduction from their family home.

"I hope these verdicts provide some measure of closure and reassurance that justice has been achieved."

News.title: PM admits cost of living help is not enough and hints at further support
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he accepts his announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Burnham told BBC's Wake up to Money he will deliver an "accumulation of smaller things" that "combine to take the pressure down" on household budgets.

He spoke of an overhaul of train fares and "more public control" of energy, water and housing but did not give details on how he would bring this about.

Burnham has made a number of announcements to help people with the cost of living since taking office, including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to 'subscription traps'.

Asked whether the changes he had announced were not significant to people struggling, he said: "I can accept criticism that this isn't enough, because I wouldn't say it's enough.

"But I take an approach to politics where I do what I can, when I can. Just take that little bit of pressure off and address an issue that you know needs addressing.

"It's not the end of the story," he added.

The prime minister, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, said he believed "more public control of essential services" such as water, energy and housing, "would mean we could get to a more substantial answer to the cost of living crisis".

On water, he said it would not be easy to reverse the privatisation of water companies in England and Wales that took place in the 1980s.

"But very much, I'm looking at what can be done. Same with energy."

He also said that, following the return of rail operators to public ownership, he wanted to "remodel the rail fares so that we can get more public benefit for people".

It comes as the government said on Wednesday that people living within 1,600ft (500m) of new upgraded electricity pylons and substations across Britain will receive a Â£250 annual discount on their bills for a decade.

News.title: Children as young as nine hurt in growing number of e-scooter crashes
News.content:
Most of the incidents in Manchester, Liverpool and Sheffield involved private e-scooters, often on public roads, pavements or footpaths, despite that being illegal.

Private e-scooters are meant only for use on private land, with the owner's permission.

Half of the children injured were aged between 10 and 13. Nearly two-thirds were boys.

Most injuries were sustained by the rider - only 5% were pedestrians that had been hit by an e-scooter - and the most common cause was falling off the e-scooter.

Around 11% were collisions with a vehicle, which was often linked to more serious injuries.

Injuries to the arms and legs were the most common, followed by head or facial injuries.

The doctors say tougher laws are urgently needed. Helmet use is not mandatory in the UK, unlike some other countries.

Some have described the private e-scooter situation in the UK as the "Wild West" with few following any rules.

The researchers told the Emergency Medicine Journal that schools, local councils, youth groups and road safety campaigns all have a role to play.

"Clearly, reporting these accidents is important to influence and change policy, but there must also be an onus on retailers to clearly advise customers of the law, and policymakers to regulate private e-scooters, such as with speed limiters, or mandate helmet use," they say.

To legally rent an e-scooter in the UK, which can be used on roads and cycle lanes, you must be at least 16 and hold a full or provisional driving licence, and the rental company must provide appropriate insurance. Rental e-scooters typically have a limited top speed of around 15mph.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: "These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads.

"It is illegal for private e-scooters to be used on roads, pavements or in other public spaces, including by under 16s, and we're bringing forward new laws to make their use safe and legal, including consulting on requirements like helmets."

News.title: Peatland fire like 'boiling in the bag' for crews
News.content:
A fire chief has said temperatures faced by crews tackling a peatland wildfire are so high they feel like "boil in the bag" meals.

The blaze at Holme Fen Nature Reserve, near Peterborough, broke out on Saturday, the second fire there in just two weeks.

Area commander Wayne Swales said about 50% of the 660-acre (270-hectare) site had been burnt - and temperatures were up to 60C (140F).

"It's indescribable in the centre: you've got peat on fire, you've got trees falling down around you, so we've not only got to try and deal with the fire, we've got to make sure our people are safe," he added.

Swales said firefighters were facing "some of the most difficult working conditions".

News.title: Boy, four, taken to hospital after Shein fake squishy toy explodes in his face
News.content:
A mum says she feels "guilty" for buying a fake squishy toy that exploded in her son's face, resulting in him needing hospital treatment.

Jodanna Bevan bought the toys from Shein for her children after seeing them discounted.

Hudson, four, was squeezing his when it "popped and exploded all over his face", with Jodanna describing the filling as a "thick white substance" with a sandy texture.

While his bloodshot eyes "seemed OK" after washing them, Jodanna said by the next morning they were extremely swollen and he was unable to open them, so she took Hudson to hospital.

Shein said it took the claims seriously and the product was no longer available on its platform.

Hudson needed water flushed through each eye to correct their pH balance, and Jodanna, from Bridgend, said it was "horrendous as a parent to watch him go through that".

She said Hudson's vision was damaged but he was given eye drops to fix it.

Hudson, like children across the UK, was drawn to the toys after they became a sensation on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube.

They often resemble dumplings, but children "can't see what's inside the box so they're excited to see which one they get".

Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned that Moscow will retaliate in kind should European nations begin seizing Russian commercial ships, while the commander of Russia's Pacific Fleet stated his personnel stand prepared to "inspect and detain" foreign boats.

Speaking while supervising naval exercises in eastern Russia, Putin issued the warning as the European Union steps up action against Moscow's covert shadow fleet, broadening sanctions to encompass hundreds of vessels and stopping individual vessels alongside their crews.

A number of European states have confirmed they are considering stricter maritime intervention protocols to target vessels believed to be circumventing trade sanctions.

Italian-led EU force boards sanctioned tanker from Russia's 'shadow fleet' in Mediterranean ( Reuters )

"We can see that the ​authorities ⁠of certain countries, in violation of international maritime law, are attempting to restrict the movement of our economic operators’ vessels..., and have recently gone so far ⁠as to consider the possibility of seizing our vessels and selling off the property ​they ⁠have plundered from us," said Putin.

"Naturally, this ‌is nothing less than piracy and robbery. And if this begins to be put into practice, we shall be forced to respond in kind. And not necessarily in ‌those waters where raids on our ships and vessels are ‌planned, but wherever we ourselves deem it necessary and appropriate."

Viktor Liina, commander of Russia's Pacific Fleet, told Putin that what he described as hostile countries like Britain and France also transported goods on vessels flying flags ⁠of convenience which - if the EU and Britain's own language was used - could also be described as a "shadow fleet."

"Western states are actively using vessels flying the flags of third countries to transport cargo in their own interests. In essence, this constitutes their shadow fleet," Liina told Putin.

"We have the capabilities to inspect and detain vessels belonging to unfriendly states and their shadow fleet; inter-agency coordination is in place, and we are ready to tackle ‌these tasks."

He said his fleet had carried out a detailed analysis of maritime ​traffic in the Asia-Pacific region and knew the routes, the cargo, and ‌ownership of the vessels. Putin also accused ⁠NATO of threatening behaviour in the Asia-Pacific region, and of creating tension in ⁠the Arctic.

"We can see that, unfortunately, the potential for conflict is growing here; NATO is making inroads here; ‌new military-political blocs are being ​formed; and new weapons systems are being deployed ‌here, or are planned for deployment, which ​also pose a threat to our country," said Putin.

It’s once again primary night in America. Minnesota, Connecticut, Vermont and Wisconsin will all hold primaries in their states. In addition, Alabama will hold primaries for its newly redrawn congressional map while South Carolina will hold a primary to replace Sen. Lindsey Graham on the Republican ballot.

All of these will set the stage for contests this November. But as any political junkie knows, once the midterms end, the presidential jockeying begins. Republicans seem firmly set on running either Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio to succeed Donald Trump.

That leaves the real contest — on the Democratic side. Earlier this year, Democrats moved their primary calendar for the Big-Six states before Super Tuesday. South Carolina will now go first, followed by Nevada, then New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and finally Virginia.

This will fundamentally alter the political calculus of any would-be candidate for the White House. As soon as the final ballots for the midterms are counted, it will be time to weigh the pros and cons of a presidential contest. Here is a list of potential candidates and why they should and should not run.

open image in gallery No matter what anyone says, former Vice President Kamala Harris is the current Democratic frontrunner in the invisible primary. ( Getty )

Former Vice President Kamala Harris

There’s no other way around it. By virtue of her being the most recent Democratic presidential nominee and someone who had to assemble a campaign within 107 days, she is the frontrunner. Just in the same way Joe Biden ran for president after Trump’s second term when voters were nostalgic for Barack Obama, Harris could easily swoop in offering a familiar product as some voters seek a return to the relative calm of the brief Biden era.

Why she should run: The new primary calendar puts South Carolina at the top. That means Black voters, particularly older female voters in that group, will likely turn out in droves for Harris. More likely than not, she will earn the endorsement of former House Majority Whip James Clyburn, the kingmaker whose nod made Hillary Clinton and Biden the respective nominees of 2016 and 2020. As Trump’s most recent opponent, she can easily call back to her warnings about the president.

Why she should think twice: Harris has never won a competitive presidential primary. She dropped out in 2019 and didn’t even make it to Iowa. Biden and Clyburn all but gifted her the Democratic nomination after Biden dropped out in 2024. And the fact remains, she still lost to Trump. All of this would make it extraordinarily hard to convince people that she should be the nominee again in a time when many voters want something new.

open image in gallery Biden’s Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg has become an effective surrogate for Democrats. But it remains uncertain if he can win over Black voters. ( Reuters )

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg

When Buttigieg ran for president in 2019, he started out as the mayor of South Bend, Indiana with a funny-sounding last name. Six years later, he now has some experience under his belt as Secretary of Transportation during the Biden administration and a trusted surrogate for Democrats. Now married with a husband and children, with some facial hair to boot, he is already heading to New Hampshire and campaigning for Democrats in his new home state of Michigan.

Why he should run: Buttigieg is an effective communicator, being one of the few Democrats willing to go on Fox News to refute talking points. Still young at 44, he could make an argument that he can be a changing of the guard in a party dominated by senior citizens.

Why he should think twice: The fact South Carolina is now the first state in the primary contests puts Buttigieg at a significant disadvantage. While he won Iowa in 2020 in a coin toss with Sen. Bernie Sanders, he placed fourth behind Tom Steyer in South Carolina. While Clyburn suggested he could be a running mate to Harris in 2024 and she said in her memoir that she wanted to make him her running mate, he still needs to earn the trust of African American voters. And his nickname, “Mayor Pete,” also gives away he’s never held statewide office before.

And the fact remains that Buttigieg, and any other openly gay candidate, would still face stigma at the ballot box. In June, he revealed that he was separated from his children after someone filed a malicious false police report against him.

open image in gallery Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) faces an important question: seek the White House or run for Senate. ( Getty )

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.)

Perhaps no potential candidate has garnered as much buzz during the midterm cycle as the four-term democratic socialist from the Bronx and Queens. Eight years ago, she shocked the nation as an insurgent candidate who beat the chairman of the House Democratic Caucus in a primary. Now in her fourth term in the House, she’s a sought-after surrogate for Democrats of all stripes. She no longer rules out running for president, and also made some people wonder what her next steps would be when she announced she would be freezing her eggs.

Why she should run: Six years ago, Ocasio-Cortez served as Sanders’ surrogate in the primary, only to see the Vermont socialist get crushed in the South. This year, progressives have made significant gains. Her socialist ally Zohran Mamdani became the mayor of New York City and socialists won insurgent primaries across the country. She also bet big when she endorsed Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate primary and he won. Michigan will now be fifth on the calendar and she can also likely coalesce support among Hispanic voters in Nevada, which will go second, alongside New Mexico.

Why she should think twice: There might be a more attractive and attainable prize on the horizon in the near future: Sen. Chuck Schumer’s seat. Whether in a primary challenge or in an open race, Ocasio-Cortez will easily coalesce support in New York and elsewhere. In New York City, the Democratic Socialists of America’s army of door-knockers will easily boost her campaign. And while she led a poll in New Hampshire, barely beating Buttigieg, that might be irrelevant considering the Granite State goes third now.

open image in gallery Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is hoping to run up the scoreboard in his re-election campaign. But his moderate record and history of support for Israel might trip him up. ( Reuters )

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro

Perhaps no candidate looks better “on paper” than Shapiro. Governor of the ultimate swing state, who won his first race by double digits, he barely hides his ambitions to be the first Jewish president of the United States. His re-election campaign is essentially a presidential campaign-in-waiting at this point.

Why he should run: He’s the governor of Pennsylvania. That alone should be enough at a time when Democrats need to put the Keystone State back in their column. Some Democrats have wondered if Harris would have won Pennsylvania had she made Shapiro, rather than Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, her running mate. Shapiro has earned plaudits for his quick repair of the I-95 bridge and his crossover appeal in a state where races go down to the wire.

Why he should think twice: Shapiro bears striking resemblance to popular governors of yore who perform well in their home state, but not under the bright lights. See also Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in 2024, New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie in 2016 and Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker in 2016. Shapiro’s longstanding support for Israel might also turn off some voters in a time when many Democratic voters simply do not trust the Israeli government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Ironically, Shapiro, who practices conservative Judaism, is less of a hawk than fellow Pennsylvanian Sen. John Fetterman.

open image in gallery California Gov. Gavin Newsom has fallen in the rankings, but still in the hunt. ( Getty )

California Gov. Gavin Newsom

About a year ago, Gavin Newsom seemed like a front-of-the-pack candidate for the 2028 nomination. His regular fights with Trump and his decision to put a ballot initiative to allow for a one-time redraw of California’s maps had him taking on the president at every turn. That, combined with his consistent jabs on social made him a hero. But since then, he has somewhat come down to Earth. Nevertheless, Newsom wears his ambition as obviously as the hair gel in his coif.

Why he should run: The best argument Newsom has is that he could argue it takes a bully to take on the mean-spirited-ness of the post-Trump MAGA movement. His term expires this year and he will not be constrained by his day job obligations the way some others will.

Why he should think twice: Newsom’s years as mayor of San Francisco, lieutenant governor and governor of California means he has years of political baggage. He survived a recall in 2021 after he was caught at a restaurant without a mask during the Covid-19 pandemic. Republicans, and even some Democrats, will be quick to point to California’s exorbitant cost of living and homelessness problem.

Newsom also poses the question of how much scandal the Democratic electorate will tolerate. Most recently, Ruby Rippey, who worked for Newsom when he was mayor of San Francisco and was married to his campaign manager and friend, published an essay about their affair that nearly tore her life apart.

open image in gallery Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear fits the profile of a fresh-faced young governor. But he also has a comparatively low-profile. ( AFP/Getty )

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear

The last one on the list was also in the running to become Harris’ running mate. Beshear has been sort of busy lately dealing with the issue of his state’s senior senator Mitch McConnell going missing in action and not disclosing details about his health. But Beshear as the chairman of the Democratic Governors’ Association is traveling the country, including in important states like South Carolina, Nevada and Michigan, where he gets important facetime with voters, donors and party activists.

Why he should run: As a relatively fresh face, Beshear can be the candidate of change and would earn the support of organized labor in states like Michigan and potentially in South Carolina. He can also make the case that he won twice in one of the deepest red state in the country and faced fierce opposition in the legislature.

Why he should think twice: Every argument for why he should run can be turned around to be a reason he should not run. Yes, he won in deep-red Kentucky, but he did so in off-year low-turnout elections. Yes, he fought with the Republican-controlled legislature, but that means he has not accomplished much in terms of a partisan wishlist. Yes, he’s the fresher face, but that means most people don’t know who he is.

Of course, this isn’t even a full list. Some like Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) have weighed whether their newfound fame could be enough to boost a presidential run. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) denies he will run, but that might change depending on if he wins re-election in Georgia and by how much. But every would-be candidate has their internal reasons to run and to pass. Consider this just a cheat sheet.

Flights across Europe continue to be disrupted as Sicily’s Mount Etna continues to erupt.

Many flights departing Catania Airport have been cancelled due to the volcanic ash, including services to Amsterdam, Paris and New York JFK.

The airport, which is located on the island of Sicily, is Italy’s fifth busiest and subject to frequent disruption due to regular activity from Etna.

The most recent update on Catania Airport’s website dated today (12 August) states: “Due to Etna’s eruptive activity and current wind conditions, Sector B3 has been closed. Arrivals and departures are suspended until 6:00 PM.”

It adds: “Passengers are kindly advised to check the status of their flight with their airline before heading to the airport. Further updates will follow in the coming hours.”

Some flights have departed and arrived according to Flight Radar data, which indicates that 10 per cent of flights are operating.

Mount Etna’s recent activity has also caused travel chaos further afield, with flights cancelled due to its ash cloud.

A statement on Malta International Airport’s website dated 11 August confirmed that it was experiencing “flight disruptions” due to Etna. The small Mediterranean island is located 220km south of Etna. Passengers are advised to check the status of their flight before travelling to the airport.

While current departures and arrivals appear to be running as normal, there are some cancellations and delays for flights to Edinburgh and Paris.

The latest update from the National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology (INGV), Etna Observatory, reports “continuing effusive activity” from eruptive vents.

Its Volcano Observatory Notice for Aviation (VONA) remains red – the highest alert – indicating ongoing hazards for aircraft from ash emissions.

In July, all flights to and from the airport were cancelled following a similar eruption.
