World.title: ‘Are we being completely gaslit?’ The slow and then sudden demise of an A-League champion
World.content:
SportSoccerAustralian soccer ‘Are we being completely gaslit?’ The slow and then sudden demise of an A-League champion Bridget McArthur August 12, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On a cold, grey day in Melbourne, between a cow paddock and a housing estate, the dream of an A-League soccer club for the west was being dismantled piece by piece. Over the past year, Western United has rivalled Forty Winks for the number of times it has been declared on the brink of closing down, yet fans, staff and players have remained optimistic. Removalists took what they could from Western United’s home ground on Tuesday after the club was wound up in insolvency. Jason South On Tuesday, the sword of Damocles finally dropped. The club was wound up in insolvency with a liquidator appointed in Federal Court, one day after the Australian Professional Leagues (APL) terminated its licence, citing several breaches to its participation agreement. Within hours, removalists entered the club’s home ground in Tarneit, taking what they could on the instructions of receiver Alvarez and Marsal, which recently took control of Western United’s parent company, WMG Holdings, on behalf of Johnson Controls, which had lent money to the club’s owners and is now seeking to recoup costs.



Vusumizi Gumbo watched from the sidelines, shaking his head. His two sons, 16-year-old Akim and 12-year-old Amiel, were supposed to be training there that night as part of Western United’s academy – one of Victoria’s largest and most affordable elite soccer pathways – which has continued operating out of Ironbark Fields and competing in the Victorian Premier League (VPL) while the A-League men’s and women’s teams have been in hibernation. Gumbo said the club had made a positive difference in Melbourne’s multicultural western suburbs. Vusumizi Gumbo’s two sons, who are academy players for Western United, have been left in limbo after the club was wound up. Jason South “There are coaches here giving their time for free to coach these kids,” he said. “It’s not only about kicking football. They are trying to instil values that are important into the community.” In recent weeks, as things have crumbled around them, the aspiring footballers have continued to train. People involved with the club have paid from their own pockets to keep the generators running.



Senior academy player Mark Leonard said it had been a strange year, with coaches and more than a dozen teammates leaving midway through, but several had stuck it out. “I think we’re 11th, but the past couple weeks we’ve been fighting, we’ve been doing really well for the situation we’ve been put in … I don’t think anyone expected us to keep up the fight,” the 20-year-old said. When this masthead spoke to Leonard on Wednesday afternoon, he believed the team would be allowed to play out the remainder of the season, with only three matches left. But just a few hours later, academy players and their families received an email informing them they had played their last games together. Football Victoria said that, as the club was being wound up in insolvency, a number of policies and regulations had been triggered that could not be overcome or breached. “Ultimately, this means WUFC teams will not be able to play further FV competition fixtures this season or into the future, effective immediately,” Football Victoria’s chief executive Dan Birrell wrote. “We know this news marks the end of an era; but we know the friendships and bond of your football community will endure.” Reacting to the news, Gumbo said he was devastated. “Tears in my house,” he said.



Tradespeople have been busy pulling apart Ironbark Fields this week after Western United was officially wound up. Jason South Loyal staff left out of pocket Academy players, staff and fans have been in limbo this past year. While almost every external indicator has pointed to the club’s imminent collapse – the dissolution of its A-League teams, the dire financial situation of its parent company and directors – the club’s higher-ups reassured them time and again: Western United, a club that produced a champion men’s team and a grand finalist women’s team in just a few years, was here to stay. As recently as last week, current and former employees – many of whom are owed more than six months’ worth of back pay – were holding out hope that one of several wealthy white knights who had expressed interest in buying the club might pull through with a rescue deal. Even after the licence was terminated, Western United continued to push an optimistic narrative, releasing a statement on Monday saying that it marked “a significant moment in our history and the beginning of a new chapter”.



“Over recent months, we have worked closely with the APL on a pathway that gives the club the best opportunity to survive, rebuild and return to the A-League under new ownership,” it said. Western United won the 2022 A-League Men grand final. Getty Australia “This creates an opportunity for new custodians, new investment and a fresh start. The objective must now be to preserve Western United’s identity in Melbourne’s west and work towards a return to the A-League for the 2027/28 season.” Staff, however, took a less rosy view. While there is a strong possibility the APL could resell the licence to one of the buyers who had previously expressed interest, and potentially reboot Western United under the same name in the same location, former employees will remain out of pocket. Related Article A-League Men Control of A-League club stripped from businessman alleged to have stolen millions from Scott Pendlebury



The club being wound up means staff have to recover lost entitlements via the federal government’s Fair Entitlements Guarantee. Under this scheme, they are entitled to recoup up to 13 weeks in unpaid wages, annual leave, long service leave, and a capped amount of redundancy pay. It does not cover unpaid superannuation, nor workers on temporary visas. One employee, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said he had not been paid for about six months and was owed roughly $30,000, some of which he would not get back. “Thankfully, I’m still living at home,” he said. “I don’t have bills, dependants, things like that, so aside from rapidly declining mental health, living-wise, I haven’t really been impacted. But others have. There are single parents, parents of young children, who have lost significant amounts in back pay and super.” Another former staff member, also speaking on the condition of anonymity, said as much as she was frustrated by the situation, she felt Steve Horvat – the former Socceroo who founded the club and remained a director until the end – had been doing everything he could to keep the club together. “Steve is probably wearing rose-coloured glasses. His dream has been this club,” she said.



“But then, we’ve been told for months and months it would be OK, so we didn’t go to media or get lawyers involved. And it’s like, are we being completely gaslit? “And what was that statement? How can they say this isn’t the end for the club? Unless part of the plan is that Western [United] will continue under different ownership … It would be a weird situation if a billionaire takes over, and it’s bustling in the future and these 40-odd staff have just been screwed over … I feel for the fans, too. The fans we did have were so passionate … It was an important club for the west.” Downfall of a dream While Western United was Horvat’s dream, it was Jason Sourasis – then a player manager for athletes including AFL legend Scott Pendlebury – who was largely bankrolling the project, including the wider Wyndham Stadium Precinct that was central to the club’s long-term future. Pitched as a combined sporting, entertainment, health and retail precinct in Melbourne’s west, featuring a 15,000-seat soccer stadium, it secured the backing of the City of Wyndham, which owns the land.



But WMG Holdings subsequently altered the proposal to be more within its means – changes the council rejected, issuing a default notice for its failure to deliver the precinct in line with what was agreed. The redevelopment of Ironbark Fields in Tarneit was central to the club’s future. Getty Images In a statement on Tuesday, Wyndham City’s director of corporate services, Mark Rossiter, said the council had gone “above and beyond” to afford the company “significant flexibility”, but it had failed to rectify the issues, which constituted a “serious breach” of the development agreement. He said the council had made the call to terminate the deal following the APL’s decision to pull the club’s licence. With the club and precinct project both in tatters, it is still unclear exactly what went so badly wrong for the club and almost everyone affiliated with it to lose significant amounts of money. The co-directors of both parent company and club, Sourasis and Horvat, are also victims after borrowing money to prop up Western United. As of March last year, Horvat owed the ATO close to $11 million – he never filed a defence and a default judgment was entered against him – while Sourasis has been embroiled in several lawsuits with angry creditors seeking recompense including Pendlebury, who alleges Sourasis invested his money in the club without his consent.



Sourasis denies the allegations and is defending the claims. Horvat declined to comment. Western United was a dream of former Socceroo Steve Horvat, pictured here playing in a match between Scotland and Australia in 1996. Getty Images Alvarez and Marsal’s senior director of restructuring, Daniel Linaker, said the biggest asset the club owned was the licence, which was bought for about $18 million but was now worth about $10 million. With that terminated, he said, there were minimal assets that could be recovered. Related Article A-League Men ‘We are sorry’: Players released as Western United placed in A-League ‘hibernation’ mode Equipment collected from the club this week was worth up to $200,000, he said – small fry compared with the $74 million debt owed. Much of the club’s money was spent on infrastructure on council land which could not be extracted.



Linaker said it was highly likely the majority of money would not be recovered. An APL spokesman said it had given the club as much time as it could to work through its financial, governance and legal matters. He said the governing body could not share specifics about the breaches mentioned in its statement that led to the club losing its licence. As for the licence, the APL said its board was considering what to do with it. Speculation regarding South Melbourne buying it have been dismissed by sources close to the APL. The National Soccer League club – which has faced its own financial battles over the years, including a period of voluntary administration – has been agitating for a seat at the table since the A-League was established two decades ago. Despite everything that has occurred, and the ongoing questions around his team’s future, Leonard holds out hope.



“I still do have a lot of faith in that the club will return … My dream would be to play for Western United one day.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The $4 million Sydney mansion facing partial demolition after bitter council feud
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWProperty development The $4 million Sydney mansion facing partial demolition after bitter council feud Carrie Fellner August 12, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney builder Christopher Ghaleb was convinced he was onto a winner. Cap in hand, he fronted the judges on Channel Ten’s Shark Tank to spruik his start-up in 2018. Dubbed “Lifesize Plans”, it offered home owners a life-size version of their project to walk through before construction. Christopher Ghaleb and his Strathfield build on the suburb’s “golden mile”. Artwork: Monique Westermann Sporting a hot-pink hard hat as television cameras tailed him around his building site, Ghaleb explained it would resolve the same problem he encountered on almost every job: having to change things after they were already built. But fast-forward eight years, and the entrepreneurial builder’s own home on Strathfield’s “golden mile” has become a case study in the very problem he set out to avoid.



Ghaleb has agreed to demolish and rebuild parts of his dream home to resolve one arm of a court battle with Strathfield Council, which has accused him of building it without valid approvals and relying on a certifier with a conflict of interest. The increasingly bitter brawl with the council has culminated in police applying for an apprehended violence order against Ghaleb to protect a senior council officer. Christopher Ghaleb’s new home occupies an irregular shaped block on Llandilo Avenue. Sam Mooy Ghaleb, 36, has been charged with stalking and intimidating Dylan Porter, the council’s former acting director of planning and environment. It comes after a rapid rise for Ghaleb and his wife, Cindy, who have recently completed a series of high-end property redevelopments and now have a portfolio worth nearly $16 million.



The jewel in the crown is “Wellings”, labelled one of the inner west’s most significant heritage estates, bought by Cindy Ghaleb for $7.5 million in 2021. Ghaleb would not comment on the AVO application and intimidation charges while they were before the courts, but defended his actions in relation to the Llandilo Avenue property. Construction is still under way at the Llandilo Avenue site. Sam Mooy “I think a couple of heritage houses next door, they didn’t want it, so they brought a fight to me,” he told the Herald. Ghaleb said the court dispute over the development had been resolved because he had reached a compromise with the council in the Land and Environment Court in February.



Ghaleb said he agreed to “minor” changes to the home to keep the peace with the council. “We agreed to lose less than 3 per cent of the floor area,” he said. According to a court judgment, the changes include demolishing walls to increase setbacks, deleting the arch columns from the entryway, introducing additional landscaping and privacy treatments on the windows, and changing the finishes to complement the streetscape’s heritage. But a Strathfield Council spokesperson denied the matters were resolved. “The Class 4 proceedings regarding the same property have not been discontinued at this stage,” they said.



Class 4 proceedings are civil enforcement proceedings in which councils can ask the Land and Environment Court to remedy or restrain breaches of planning laws. The spokesperson noted a Building Information Certificate (BIC) had been issued for the property in June. The certificates protect unauthorised works from demolition for seven years. The saga has sparked anger and indignation on Llandilo Avenue, with several neighbours making public submissions to the council in protest. They argued the house did not sit within the heritage fabric of the street, intruded on neighbours’ privacy and retrospective approvals should not be granted legitimising unlawful works. The controversy is the latest flashpoint in an ongoing debate about whether the NSW planning regime does enough to prevent unauthorised development.



Just streets away, Strathfield Council has been fighting for years for the demolition of a mansion that was found to have been unlawfully built. Critics argue the private certification system, together with building information certificates, can allow unauthorised building work to be carried out and remain standing even when councils argue it should never have been built in the first place. Local Government NSW (LGNSW) represents the state’s councils, which are responsible for assessing the merits of BICs. LGNSW has been lobbying the state government to review the framework for BICs, arguing growing numbers of home owners are misusing them for “approving” unauthorised works. A Department of Planning spokesperson disputed that claim, saying statewide data showed no upward trend in BICs.



The spokesperson said recent reforms would ease the pressure on councils in relation to BICs by simplifying the process to make compliance easier and creating a clearer process for regulatory action and retrospective approval for unauthorised works, where appropriate. Related Article Investigation

Development outrage Fury as Sydneysiders build their mansions, then ‘ask forgiveness later’ “The reforms also introduce new offences for carrying out building work without an approval or contrary to an approval,” the spokesperson said, noting they carried maximum penalties of up to $220,000 for individuals and $1.1 million for businesses. Asked about the use of BICs, Ghaleb said he was no longer involved in development work but said it had been common for builders to use them in the past. “Builders would say, ‘I’ll do what I want,’ and then [get] a building information certificate,” he said.



“[I] wouldn’t be trying that these days, especially with Strathfield Council. They’re not there to muck around.” Purple patch While the Sharks failed to bite during Ghaleb’s television appearance, Lifesize Plans soon began to get noticed. By 2021, the business was expanding overseas, attracting glowing press coverage and had collected high-profile board members. But within a few years the company was struggling to stay afloat: it entered voluntary administration at the end of 2024 and had to be salvaged via a deed of company arrangement. In his report, administrator Daniel Frisken found the company became insolvent on June 30, 2023.



Frisken said the remaining sole director, Raymond Sheikh, had told him the business’s demise was due to the misappropriation of franchise deposits, excessive overspending, mismanagement of the company’s business and a claim brought by a creditor. Frisken said the director had not substantiated those claims with documentation, but his review of the books and records indicated the company had traded at a loss since its incorporation. Christopher Ghaleb promoting his invention on Nine News. Ghaleb has since attributed his business difficulties to severe personal trauma. In March, he told the NSW Personal Injury Commission’s review panel that he “never returned to normal and never returned to work” after developing post-traumatic stress disorder from witnessing a fatal car accident at Huntleys Point in 2019.



Ghaleb told the Herald he had stepped away from the business due to personal issues and wasn’t involved in its failure. “I wasn’t following their struggle too much at all,” he said. Sheikh said it was unfair to attribute the company’s difficulties to one individual or to characterise what occurred solely as mismanagement. He said the loss of Ghaleb’s active involvement following the accident had left those running the company with the difficult task of continuing a specialised concept “without full access to the person who had conceived [it]”. Sheikh said that, since becoming involved in 2024, he had worked to settle debts, repay franchisees and put the company on a sustainable footing, with the rebuilding process now “progressing successfully”.



Splash in the neighbourhood As his business fortunes faded, Ghaleb and his wife turned their attention to property redevelopment. In 2024, Ghaleb arrived with a splash in the neighbourhood, paying $4.1 million for a knock-down rebuild on Llandilo Avenue. Many of the street’s homes are a time capsule of the arts and crafts design era that championed natural materials and ornate details. The homes still reflect “Strathfield’s legacy as a suburb of grand homes for Sydney’s elite”, a planning document said.



Ghaleb soon set about demolishing his home, which was at the end of a long driveway and tucked behind two heritage-listed mansions, one of which was designed by renowned architect Thomas Pollard Sampson. One of the heritage-listed homes on Llandilo Avenue. Sitthixay Ditthavong To the astonishment of neighbours, a new home began to materialise where the driveway itself formerly stood. It featured a Mediterranean-inspired aesthetic, embellished with rendered white archways. Ghaleb’s consultants argued the nine-metre-wide street frontage could more than accommodate the new home, which was within a “streetscape that has undergone significant transformation due to the construction of contemporary dwellings”.



Ghaleb said he hadn’t broken any rules by relocating the house, but the decision had surprised the council. An artist’s impression of the home filed with council prior to the court verdict. “For the past 50 years [the house was] at the back,” he said. “They wouldn’t expect a house at the front.” One neighbour was blindsided. “When demolition commenced, I contacted council and was told no application for demolition or development was on record,” the neighbour said in a public submission.



The project has instead been approved by a private certifier under the state government’s fast-track complying development pathway. The rear of the house, which now extends all the way to the street front. Sam Mooy Complying development certificates (CDCs) allow straightforward projects that meet prescribed standards to bypass the traditional development application process. But Strathfield Council is now fighting to have the CDC declared invalid in the Land and Environment Court. It issued a stop work order at the site in mid-2025 and filed documents with the court that have been obtained by the Herald.



In them, the council argued the dwelling failed to meet the gross floor area and minimum setbacks allowable under a CDC and its basement amounted to an unapproved third storey. Related Article Exclusive

Development outrage Tear it down or go to jail: Council escalates fight with owner of unlawful Sydney mansion The council also alleged the CDC should be struck out because of a conflict of interest. The certifier, Sandres Markhani, and his colleague, James Wardan, both presented themselves as employees of Sydney Wide Certifiers, according to the council. However, Wardan prepared the architectural plans under a different company he owned and controlled called Syd Consulting Pty Ltd, the council alleged.



“A fair-minded observer might reasonably apprehend that because of Mr Markhani’s association with Mr Wardan, Mr Markhani might not bring an impartial mind to the determination of the application for the CDC,” the council said. Related Article Development outrage The illegal mansion, the court case and the silent witness Neither Markhani nor Wardan responded to the Herald’s request for comment. Ghaleb denied he used a certifier with a conflict of interest. “People throw 300 things at something and hope two or three stick,” he said.



Private certifiers have a responsibility to take action if they identify unauthorised work, and the NSW Building Commission can take disciplinary action against them if they fail to do so. In recent weeks, Ghaleb has been busy finishing the outstanding construction works, estimated to be worth nearly half a million dollars. The stalking and intimidation matter returns to Burwood Local Court in October. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Redacting the dress code
World.content:
“Graham Russell’s friend was turned back at the Cuesta border in 1971 as his hair was too long (C8),” notes Mia David of Wollongong. “My friend was married in 1968, and, while on her honeymoon, she (dressed in a very fetching pants suit) and her husband went to a club for lunch. She was denied entry, as ladies in pants were not allowed. Not a worry. She removed the trousers, and they accepted her attire of a very short miniskirt. Apparently, she had to be extra careful as she sat down for lunch.”

“My own experience in early 1970 in Singapore was similar, but different,” says Rhod Jeffrey of Surry Hills. “I was marooned there for six weeks awaiting a money transfer. I had to renew my visa weekly where there was a sign stating: ‘Persons with long hair will be served last so as to cause them the maximum of inconvenience’. I had fairly long hair but encountered no animosity or inconvenience because of it.”

“Working as a commercial artist in Jakarta 1973, (pre-Photoshop), my job was retouching poster artwork for rock stars touring Singapore,” says Peter Barker of One Mile. “I think I’m the only person with the honour of giving Mick Jagger a short-back-and-sides for The Rolling Stones’ Pacific Tour in 1973. So horrific was my retouching, the band never made it to Singapore because the doctored publicity material made them unrecognisable!”

It’s a long way from Rhoda and Gus’ surprise Joburg snowfall of ’81 (C8), but Pauline McGinley of Drummoyne is well versed when it comes to the white stuff: “Growing up in Scotland, I spent my childhood in the snow. Fingers and toes stuffed into woollen gloves and socks. Snow days off school. When you would wake up in the morning after a nightfall of snow, you knew immediately, before even looking out the window. Quiet, hushed and an intense stillness. The joy!”

“I had a similar opera experience to Nola Tucker (C8),” recalls Elizabeth Savage of Hughes (ACT). “Berlin Opera House, L’italiana in Algeri, sung in Italian with German surtitles. No idea what the story was, but the music was pleasant, and the ballet interludes were impressive.”

World.title: ‘There was no precedent’: The moment that had Alone producers terrified
World.content:
CultureTV & radioReality TV ‘There was no precedent’: The moment that had Alone producers terrified Karl Quinn August 12, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For producers and contestants alike, making Alone is all about anticipating risks and being prepared to meet them. But as viewers of the latest season of the Australian iteration will know, this year the survival competition broke the sort of new ground nobody wanted: a contestant went missing. “It was a world first, which is why the panic levels were so high,” says executive producer Riima Daher. “There was no precedent, nothing to fall back on in this scenario.” Former refugee Arash ascribes his behaviour to going into “survival mode”. SBS When Afghanistan-born wrecking-yard worker and taekwondo champion Arash went AWOL after 26 days, Daher says, “honestly, the first thought was ‘Is he dead?’ I was absolutely terrified. You worry that something really bad has happened, the sorts of things you don’t want to think about, but the sorts of things that can happen in the woods sometimes. And you start to check the water to make sure he hasn’t fallen in there.” The Sapmi region of northern Finland, where this season was filmed, is home to bears, wolves and reindeer, all of which posed potential threats to the 10 contestants from the other end of the Earth. But Arash’s disappearance – leaving behind the GPS tracker and emergency phone he was supposed to carry at all times, as well as his camera equipment – was not down to any of those things. It was, rather, the result of some sort of brain snap.



Though he declined to answer questions from this masthead, Arash does offer some insight into what happened in the episode that aired on Wednesday night. In a voiceover as he is being extracted by boat, Arash attempts to explain what was going through his mind when he ditched everything and wandered away from his camp. “I grew up in a war zone. I crossed seven countries with no documents. I’ve been lost in the sea, slept in the jungle, and I think this experience activated a survival mode that I know the best,” he said. “And when I get in that mode, the rules do not matter. I only rely on myself. All I was thinking was just to survive.”



He labelled his behaviour a “blunder” that had cost him a “very beautiful great opportunity” to change his life by winning the $250,000 prize for whichever contestant stays the longest. “I made a mistake, and I take full responsibility for it,” he said. “That will stay with me for the rest of my life.” It will stay with Daher and her team, too. Riima Daher and team search frantically for Arash. SBS At the height of the panic, there were “about 15 or 20 people” on the ground searching for Arash. “We called on people who weren’t even part of our rescue team to help,” Daher says. The six or seven hours it took to find him was, she says, “the most scared I’ve ever been personally or professionally. You question your career choices. I’m like, ‘Why am I not just working on Love Island? Everyone’s in the villa. What am I thinking?’ And you do start to fear the worst. You start to spiral, you start to see headlines.”



Did you see yourself in the dock in a courtroom? Related Article Reality TV Alone Australia’s new season is ‘the polar opposite’ of what we’ve seen before “One hundred per cent I did, I can’t lie. And then you retrace your steps. You go, ‘Did I do everything I’m supposed to do? Where are the holes in my responsibility?’” And when you finally did locate him? “We could have killed him.” Despite the anxiety he had caused, the producers didn’t immediately want to pull Arash from the contest. “You always want to give the participants as much rope as possible,” Daher says.



The problem was, he couldn’t articulate why he had done what he had, and that cast serious questions over his mental state. “It was a serious breach,” Daher says. “I mean, it placed him in real danger, it placed all of us in danger to have to go and look for him. Had he been able to explain it in a way that made sense, perhaps we could have left him in there, but he couldn’t. “From a duty-of-care point of view – as well as a rule-break point of view – we just couldn’t put him back in.” Alone Australia is on SBS, Wednesdays from 7.30pm

World.title: Is 30 minutes in this room the secret to beating stress and burnout?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandStress management Is 30 minutes in this room the secret to beating stress and burnout? Courtney Kruk August 12, 2026 — 8:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The $6.8 trillion global wellness industry knows how to capitalise on a moment, and right now, it’s attuned to the fact that people are feeling increasingly stressed and burnt out. It’s why I wasn’t surprised when a video came across my feed for a new wellness clinic in Brisbane offering “Australia’s first high-tech nervous system reset studio”. Like stress and burnout, nervous system dysregulation is a hot topic, and in the information age, once a trend seeps into the collective consciousness, you know a fix is waiting in the wings. Cheatcode Playground is a new wellness studio to combat stress, burnout and fatigue in Brisbane’s Fortitude Valley. Cheatcode Playground While I’m cynical about capitalism’s encroachment on the wellness industry and the pseudoscientific claims underpinning many products and practices, I suffer from stress and am perpetually exhausted.



If 30 minutes on a vibrating chair in a dark room could make a difference, I was willing to try it. What is Cheatcode Playground? Founded by Lachy and Renee Huddy, Cheatcode Playground is described as a recovery and performance centre in Fortitude Valley that uses specialised equipment “to shift how your body and mind are operating”. Each treatment room is fitted with the same devices: a vibration chair, a light-and-sound lamp, and a cellular recovery device. These are used in combination with a guided breathing program. You don’t need any prior experience and the team will tailor the session – which runs for 18 or 30 minutes – to your needs, whether that’s stress relief, energy, or a general “reset”.



For whatever reason, Cheatcode emphasises that you stay fully clothed throughout the session. The devices The tech used isn’t new, but Lachy says his team is the first in Australia to combine these specific devices in a commercial setting. The main device – the Shiftwave vibrating chair – retails for about $10,000. Not the kind of wellness gadget the average punter can afford.



According to its makers, Shiftwave uses “pulsed pressure waves and breath-guided audio to support the body’s natural stress and recovery responses, working below conscious effort to help you feel calm, clear, or ready when it matters most”. While you can control the intensity of the vibrations, it takes a minute to get used to the feeling that you might pulsate off the chair at any moment. The audio component of Shiftwave is essentially a guided meditation with breath work – someone telling you when to breathe, and at what pace and level of intensity. The Shiftwave chair combines guided breathing with low-frequency vibroacoustic stimulation. Shiftwave This happens under a stroboscopic lamp called the “roXiva RX1”. Positioned over your face, the lamp looks like an epileptic’s worst nightmare, but the idea is to close your eyes and allow flickering lights and timed sounds to guide your brainwaves into alpha and theta states.



Depending on the program, you’ll see different colours, patterns and imagery – not dissimilar to a psychedelic experience. The final device – the “NanoVI” – delivers humidified air to speed up cellular repair. After the session, Renee, who doubles as Cheatcode’s “Beverage Alchemist” whips up a coffee with a bunch of ingredients anyone who’s stepped into a Flannerys health food store would be familiar with. What the founders say Before launching their business, Renee and Lachy managed a thoroughbred farm on the Sunshine Coast, and in 2024, they wrote, produced and acted in a feature film. The stress of making the film motivated them to create Cheatcode, which opened in June.



Travis Wesley, Cheatcode’s client flow director and front-of-house manager, has a background in theatre. Lachy says they’re not making any scientific claims about what the tech can do, but they believe they’ve created a genuine experience that can combat a range of concerns. Cheatcode Playground founders Renee and Lachy Huddy, and Client Flow Director Travis Wesley. Courtney Kruk “What we sell is the shift,” Lachy says. “The world that we have constructed is simply not good for the human nervous system. Stress is a natural part of life; constant stress is not.



“The issue is no one can switch off any more … and that’s part of what we want to address.” Related Article Perspective

Trends Neck-deep in freezing water in West End, I wanted the cold truth Renee says the beginner-friendly nature of the service is part of its appeal, with many people struggling to master activities that help them switch off. “[A lot of people] find meditation really hard. It’s one more skill to learn,” she says. “I find it funny that we have invented all of this tech to just take us back to if we lived as cavemen, not doing all of these things. That’s the state we’re trying to get to.”



Wesley adds that the $59 service (for first-time users) is accessible to those who would never otherwise afford the devices. “We want it to be accessible because everyone has burnout,” he says. What the research says Studies exploring controlled breath work practices show it can reduce stress and anxiety and improve mood. The roXiva light lamp offers drug-free psychedelic trips. It’s a fun experience but the scientific benefits are unclear. roXiva



Stroboscopic light stimulation research is emerging, but there is some evidence that consistent use can impact depression, insomnia and cognitive functions such as memory and attention. Related Article Wellbeing Beware the bad advice: With huge profits on the line, our wellness pin-ups have changed Research conducted by Shiftwave, including on police officers and first-responders, has shown positive results, with participants reporting lower work-related stress after sessions, and reduced tension. But this has not been peer-reviewed, so take it with a grain of salt. There’s no evidence for Cheatcode Playground’s approach of using all the devices in unison, only studies supporting the tech in isolation. The verdict



Parts of the session that I was sure would be uncomfortable and overstimulating – like the lamp – were pleasantly surprising. Other aspects bordered on too intense or were distracting. Related Article Mental health ‘Not snowflakes’: Severe mental disorders surge among young people At times my mind, which I had hoped would enter a blissful state of surrender, wandered incessantly, and there were moments where I felt panicked about work or things around the house that needed fixing. I felt a buzz immediately after the session, a bit like stepping off a rollercoaster, and I was grateful to be quarantined from my devices for 30 minutes. While I was optimistic that the session would result in an exceptional night’s sleep and unlock creative excellence, that wasn’t my experience, and the stress and anxiety I tried to overcome returned with a vengeance the next day.



Maybe if the schedules were reversed – a session after a particularly stressful event – the outcome would have been different. After only one session, it’s hard to deliver a concrete verdict. I’m not sure I’ll be back, but would recommend the experience to the wellness-curious crowd. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The demonisation of migrants needs to be debunked
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters The demonisation of migrants needs to be debunked August 12, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Barnaby Joyce’s recent contribution to the migration debate: ″⁣you meet (migrants) when you’re trying to drive a car to work. That’s why you can’t get anywhere″⁣ (″⁣Hanson hits out at Burke on migration numbers″⁣, 11/8) is a demonisation of migrants that is as offensive as his previous claim that ″⁣people who look like they’ve recently arrived″⁣ are knocking Australian-born residents out of home auctions. On The Bolt Report, he said that One Nation’s foreign ownership policy applied to permanent residents only to correct the record minutes later: ″⁣No, we are not going to be kicking permanent residents out of their house.″⁣ Joyce and Pauline Hanson want you to believe foreign ownership of residential property is out of control, but the reality is very different with less than 1 per cent of dwellings acquired by foreign persons in each of the past three years. The sooner Tony Burke releases his oversight of migration policy, the sooner Labor can debunk One Nation’s migration nonsense.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne Victoria doesn’t require circuses

The rulers of ancient Rome kept the people happy by providing them with bread and circuses. Our Victorian rulers provide us with plenty of circuses. Money has been thrown away on games recently played somewhere north of Hadrian’s Wall, $100 million or so is expended each year on a motorised chariot race and $395 million is to be lavished on something called a pit stop that is associated with that race and now another $10.7-15 million is to be tossed to American gladiators to play a football game with rules that are probably incomprehensible to most of us. Unfortunately our rulers show little interest in supplying us with bread in the form of essentials such as adequately funded hospitals, schools and judicial services and appropriate numbers of police. As to our roads, no prudent Roman would think of risking his chariot by driving on them. It will be fitting if (notwithstanding the recent palace revolution) our profligate rulers are thrown to the lions next election.

Arthur Roberts, Elwood Opposition by name, and nature

The opposition wants a police investigation as to how a critical note from the Japanese government about Anthony Albanese and crown melons was leaked to the press. On one hand, the opposition are ecstatic about having the information to beat Albanese over the head, and on the other hand they want an investigation to work out how it became public in the first place. The opposition is always looking for a way to criticise the government, even if it is trivial in the extreme.

Alan Inchley, Frankston



Howard’s way is hard to define

What exactly does John Howard mean when he says this lot is miserable and rotten (″⁣Liberals must ‘do the work’ to tackle One Nation: ex-PM″⁣, 12/8)? If he used the principle of Logos and articulated in more accurate terms what he thinks the current government is doing incorrectly, his desperate plea for Liberal voters to stop defecting to One Nation might have validity. Just what does he mean when he says Angus Taylor and his party should be the best demonstration of themselves? I think they’re doing very well at that already.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson Listen to the experts in their field

The degree of civility of a society can be reflected on how it treats its mentally infirm. Professor Pat McGorry’s desperate plea (Comment, 12/8) for the government to revitalise its initial good work after the 2018 royal commission into Victoria’s mental health system is timely for the new Labor premier to add to his list of genuine problems such as potholes in Victoria, rather than confected ones, to fix (″⁣Business wins over Carroll on WFH″⁣, 12/8). Politicians please listen and act on pleas and advice from professional experts rather than playing politics that will affect real lives of the infirm and their love ones in Victoria and Australia.

Yean Lim, Toorak THE FORUM A lovely thought

Sixty million dollars to expand their school? (″⁣Scotch College in talks to buy Vision Australia HQ in $60m expansion″⁣, 12/8) How lovely. A 2024 total income of more than $87 million? Fine.

Scotch College is obviously not a struggling school, so how about redirecting their $9 million from government sources to under-resourced or dilapidated public schools where it would help more students? Scotch College could bask in the knowledge that its charity had helped thousands.

I know, ″⁣Tell her she’s dreaming″⁣. But wouldn’t it be lovely?

Julie Moffat, St Leonards Stop the largesse

News that Scotch College is about to spend $60 million on buying Vision Australia’s unused site says everything we need to know about education funding in Australia. While public schools fall into disrepair and class sizes grow, these massive private entities expand ever more with obscene amounts drawn from the public purse. When does this largesse stop?

Hans Pieterse, Narre Warren North



Funding makes no sense

When a private school can well afford $60 million to buy a property to expand, what is the reason for government funding from the public purse of $9 million? Surely the state school system has greater need for scarce resources than an elite school that few can afford to attend. Unfortunately the major parties are not interested in redressing this inequality.

It is a disgrace.

Geraldine Lakha, Balwyn North Carving up the AFL

Curiously, the latest crisis within the AFL makes me think of food: If represented by a pie chart, the most significant slice would be ″⁣damage control″⁣, with relatively minor serves of transparency and accountability, and a popular dessert at AFL House would surely be fudge.

Bruce Watson, Belgrave Suburban memories

Having lived most of my long life in Melbourne, and some of it in suburbs close to Elsternwick, I was keenly interested in the piece from the Life in the Burbs series on Elsternwick.

On many occasions I have driven into or through Elsternwick for shopping or business reasons, and in earlier days pushed my bicycle to visit friends.

I, too, could identify with its diversity. My mother’s family had lived in several Elsternwick locations and were conscious of the many impressive properties developed in the land boom of the late 1800s, some of which survived the subsequent land crash and are still there today, such as the spectacular Ripponlea estate.

Another less-favoured part of the suburb was brought to light by the author George Johnston who lived his early life there. His acclaimed novel My Brother Jack was based on growing up in Elsternwick and has been described as the best account of life in Melbourne between the two world wars, including the Great Depression and its effects on suburban life.

Peter Le Get, Heathmont Other icons

As a resident of Elsternwick for many years before a seachange some years ago, it was interesting to read Phil Noble’s extensive view of the suburb (″⁣Diversity keeps suburb grounded″⁣, 11/8).

The fact that I still return there at least a few times every month shows how the attraction of Elsternwick Noble writes about is certainly still there. It was a bit disappointing, however, that Noble hadn’t highlighted three other iconic Elsternwick establishments: AVIV Cakes and Bagels, Blights Shoe Repairs (& discount tobacconist) with Wesley and Jane, and The Avenue (once Sunflower) Bookstore.

Bernard Daly, Flinders What is the other?

Your correspondent (Letters, 11/8), confides that he once thought of himself as a doctor battling an epidemic in his role as a journal’s sub-editor struggling to repel grammatical and spelling errors.

There is no such consolation for me, as every night I am assailed by solecisms on television news services whose editors ought to know better.

Unlike your correspondent, no drinking of coffee or listening to jazz can comfort me, not even a draught of Keats or his ″⁣beaker full of the warm South″⁣ (Clare Valley shiraz), can placate me as I listen, night after night, on ABC and SBS evening news, to the announcer informing me that, in the war between Putin and the Ukraine, and the one between Trump and Iran, ″⁣both sides are blaming the other″⁣. When are they going to reveal the identity of this mysterious third party – ″⁣the other″⁣?

Dr Trevor Hay, Montmorency



Turning American

Thanks to your correspondent for their comments on the appalling state of what once was English in today’s Australia (Letters, 10/8). To this Americanisation, we can add the phrases , “kick the can down the road”, “off-ramp”, “double down” and other US inanities.

Ian Usman Lewis, Armidale, NSW Keep it at arm’s length

Further to the discussion of the complication of simple English terms, (Letters, 10/8) what about the term ″⁣reaching out″⁣? When someone invites me to ″⁣reach out″⁣ to them, I always reply that my arms aren’t long enough but that I’m happy, if needed, to contact them.

Mary Walker, Richmond Gambolling along

So many letters full of doom and gloom. Things are looking up. The potholes along my regular route now have bright yellow rings painted round them, while federally, according to an ABC news reader, Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor are meeting in a bipartisan approach to the issue of problem gambollers.

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East Industry demands

Ehsan Noroozinejad (“Australia’s megaproject boom may deepen housing crux”, 11/8) articulates the demands that all forms of infrastructure construction make on the finite supply of workers and materials. He makes it clear that Australia is struggling to meet its housing construction targets due to the massive pipeline of projects across electricity transmission, transport, schools and sporting venues.

Noroozinejad makes good suggestions for co-ordinated planning, increased apprenticeships, more community housing, and other initiatives. Tellingly, he states that the infrastructure workforce shortfall ″⁣could exceed 300,000 by mid-2027″. He warns that if the government cuts immigration, this shortfall will be worse.

Andrew Trembath, Blackburn PM, be quiet

What Anthony Albanese needs to do about the Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi melon brouhaha is apologise to Takaichi privately, then be quiet on the matter. And tell his ministers to be quiet about it also.

Everyone who has seen the video (and who hasn’t now?) would see the innuendo. There is no amount of spin that makes this episode look anything but tawdry.

Danny Cole, California Gully



Fire season funding

The fires in Europe and Canada do not augur well for our coming summer. Let’s hope our fire services have all the funds they need to procure vehicles and equipment to give their staff the best chance against bushfires.

John Walsh, Watsonia Safety comes first

I was a union rep at an underground mine in the 1970s. This was at a time when it was a common practice to pay miners extra money for working in bad ground. This was called danger money.

The union successfully fought to outlaw the practice as the incentive prioritised ongoing production over safety. The dilemma for AFL clubs and concussion is remarkably similar. Miners are fully aware of the risks in working underground. They do so willingly. Playing AFL will never be risk free.

Nonetheless, there is a line where safety must be the priority. That cannot be left just up to the individual when the circumstances indicate there is an elevated risk to a player’s safety.

Tony Newport, Hillwood Poor health move

Donald Trump and Robert F. Kennedy jnr have changed the recommendations for childhood measles-mumps-rubella vaccinations in the US on the thoroughly debunked notion that the vaccination is responsible for a rise in autism.

Medical experts and commentators have widely criticised this misinformation that will have serious consequences for the public and the health of children in the US, remember the Tylenol (paracetamol) in pregnancy announcement which caused widespread anxiety?

Trump is wildly enthusiastic about leaving a legacy and memorials to himself, the legacy of this announcement will be children’s illness.

Dr Geoffrey Haughton, Sandringham An unequal society

The front page juxtaposition of ″⁣Bags of vision″⁣ and ‴⁣⁣Kids’ mental health unit shut, staff investigated″⁣ (12/8) illustrates the inequitable funding of essential services in our society albeit the funding sources of each of these are different.

Many federal government funds are means-tested, why does this not apply to the funding of private schools? If Scotch can afford to pay $60 million to fund its expansion, similarly MLC funding its new aquatic centre, even if those only used private funds surely they do not need government subsidies when public schools are crying out for adequate to fund basic things like adequate staff, repairs etc.

These two examples are just the tip of the iceberg, the inequalities in our society just grow every year,

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Roadworks

Potholed roads! There’s 5.7kilometres of bitumen around Albert Park lake in pristine condition.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill Maybe we need to have a ″⁣pothole insurance policy″⁣.

Robyn Thornton, Hamilton Local and state governments can fix the potholes and repair the roads simply by increasing taxes or by taking money from health and education. I vote for increased road-user charges.

Peter Hendrickson, East Melbourne



Furthermore

How long until Pauline Hanson uses the term “Fake News”?

Alan Williams, Port Melbourne Scotch College’s plan to buy Vision Australia’s head office in Kooyong is 60 million reasons why the Australian taxpayer should not be subsidising wealthy elite private schools (″⁣Scotch eyes Vision Australia HQ″⁣, 12/8).

Phil Alexander, Eltham The article ″⁣Secret death tax in CGT changes″⁣ (12/8) about changes to taxes on inheritance of shares is very concerning. Pressure needs to be put on government to change this legislation quickly.

Kay Moulton, Surrey Hills An NFL game for $10 to $15 million is a bargain compared to $100 million for a F1 four-day car race (″⁣A four-hour, weekday game with no parking hottest ticket in town″⁣, 12/8).

Geoff Gowers, Merricks North The proof of the pudding is in the eating, as the saying goes. Why study the ingredients offered by other candidates, when Josh Fraser has proven he can dish up success?

Merryn Boan, Brighton



Why were all the constituent components of Great Britain listed as separate countries of origin in the Census, but Wales was not?

Stephen Yolland, Doncaster (Proudly Australian – and Welsh) When will they announce the census winner?

Alejandro A. Téllez Vargas, Frankston

World.title: Finks sergeant-at-arms works on North East Link, court hears
World.content:
The alleged sergeant-at-arms of an outlaw motorcycle gang accused of being part of a trio who threatened a man with a gun has a job working on North East Link, a court has heard. Dylan Mallia, 28, faced the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday charged with affray after a confrontation at a house in Harkness. The Finks are a notorious outlaw motorcycle gang. LUIS ENRIQUE ASCUI He applied for bail, leading to his partner testifying in court that he was employed as a machine operator for Symal on the Carroll government’s $26 billion North East Link project. Former premier Jacinta Allan previously declared there was “no evidence” bikies had cashed in on the road project as she defiantly stared down calls for a royal commission into the Big Build.



But Mallia’s partner said he had worked for Symal for “five or six years”, as his defence lawyer argued his stable employment was a reason he should be granted bail. Mallia’s partner acknowledged she was aware he was part of the Finks bikie gang. Victoria’s North East Link road project is expected to open in 2028. Jason South Police allege Mallia, Isekeli Walls and another unknown person pulled up at a house on Indigo Link in a Ford Ranger and threatened a man in the property’s driveway on June 30. A police summary of allegations read out in court said CCTV had captured the unidentified person producing a silver handgun and pointing it at the victim.



Mallia and Walls then allegedly went back to their vehicle and returned with a black bag and a glass bottle. The victim armed himself with a knife, police say. A police prosecutor said Mallia picked up a ladder from the front of the property and threatened the resident with it before the trio drove away. The special operations group arrested Mallia and Walls on Tuesday. The latter appeared at the Wyndham Magistrates’ Court earlier on Wednesday and did not apply for bail. Magistrate Gerald Lethbridge released Mallia back into the community on the grounds he could spend more time awaiting trial than a potential sentence for affray. Police had opposed bail, alleging Mallia was an unacceptable risk and was the sergeant-at-arms of the Finks’ West End chapter.



“The current offending is brazen, unsophisticated and shows a contempt for the law,” the police prosecutor said. “He simply does not care for the consequences of his actions.” Lethbridge said the prosecution “will not have a lot of difficulty” proving Mallia was at the Harkness home, but noted his defence might argue he was unaware or not complicit in his co-accused brandishing a weapon. “Of course, it’s very premature,” Lethbridge said, “but it is an overwhelming prosecution case in terms of the most serious and aggravated aspects of it.” He added: “The court makes the comment that in the current context of bail being discussed very frequently out of court, there seems to be a misunderstanding as to what bail is. “Bail is a promise that somebody will attend court at a certain time at a certain place, while they are recognised as a matter of law to be innocent until they are proven guilty.”



In a statement on Wednesday evening, Symal confirmed Mallia had worked for them for five years as a plant operator involved in excavation and loading materials. A spokesperson said Symal was not aware of the charges against Mallia before being contacted by The Age, “nor any alleged involvement with a motorcycle club or any criminal activity.” This masthead has also contacted North East Link for comment.
